For a database engineer building a web app, this is the B-tree, the transaction log, some MVCC, not the C source of Postgres. For an AI engineer in 2026 building products on top of frontier LLMs, this is _what an LLM is_ , _how it generates_ , _what makes it stochastic_ , _why it hallucinates_ , _what a context window actually is_ , and _how to read a model card as if it were a spec sheet_. And then you stop. The rest belongs to Series III, where the people who actually train these things live.

This chapter gives you _exactly the right amount of inside-the-box knowledge_. By the end, when Chapter 3 puts a real API in your hands, you will know what is happening on the other side of the network call. You will not know it the way an Anthropic pretraining scientist knows it. You will know it the way an engineer needs to know it: well enough to make correct architectural decisions, not so well that you get bogged down in things you will never need on the job.


### 2.1 What an LLM actually is: the engineer's level

Let's strip it down.

A large language model is a function. The function takes a sequence of tokens (we will get to what those are in a moment) and returns a probability distribution over what the next token should be. That is the entire function signature:
    
    
    next_token_distribution = model(token_sequence)
    

Everything else (chatbots, agents, RAG, structured output, voice assistants, computer-using agents) is a wrapper around that one function. You take a sequence of tokens, you ask the model what the next token should be, the model gives you a distribution, you sample from the distribution, you append the sampled token to your sequence, and you call the model again with the longer sequence. You do this until the model emits a special token meaning _stop_ , or until you decide externally to stop (max tokens, stop sequence, your patience ran out).

That is the loop. Read the previous paragraph twice; the entire field unfolds from it. Every architectural pattern you will see in the next 23 chapters is a way of preparing the input sequence cleverly, or of constraining the output sampling cleverly, or of feeding the output back into something else cleverly. The model itself does the one job: _given a sequence, give me a distribution over the next token._

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
#### Definition: Token

A token is the unit of input and output for an LLM. It is not the same thing as a word. It is not the same thing as a character. It is the unit produced by a tokenizer, a separate piece of software trained alongside the model whose job is to chop text into a sequence of integers from a fixed vocabulary (typically 32K to 256K entries).

In plain language, this means: when you send the model the string "Hello, world!", the tokenizer first turns it into something like `[15496, 11, 1917, 0]`, four integers representing _Hello_ , _,_ , _world_ , and _!_ respectively, though the exact splits depend on the tokenizer. The model never sees text. It sees integer sequences. Every billing meter, every context-window limit, every latency measurement is denominated in tokens, not in characters or words. A useful rule of thumb for English text in 2026 is that one token is approximately 0.75 words, or four characters; for code, more like one token per 3 characters; for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, often one token per 1–2 characters. (Tokenizers differ by provider; we will see this matter in §2.6.)

This is why an LLM cannot reliably count the letter r in _strawberry_ : the model never sees the letters. It sees the token for _strawberry_ (often a single token) and is being asked, essentially, to do a calculation on a piece of data it does not have access to in the form the question implies. This is not a bug; it is a consequence of the tokenization layer that sits between text and the model.


### 2.2 Pretraining at the engineer's level

The function `model(token_sequence) -> next_token_distribution` does not come from nowhere. It is the result of a process called _pretraining_ , which is the part of LLM creation that costs tens of millions of dollars and runs for months on thousands of GPUs.

Here is the engineer's-level version of what pretraining does. Take an enormous corpus of text: trillions of tokens scraped from the web, books, code repositories, scientific papers, transcripts. For every position in the corpus, mask out the next token and ask the model to predict it from the preceding context. Penalize the model when it is wrong; tweak the model's billions of parameters slightly in the direction that would have made it less wrong. Repeat trillions of times.

That is it. The model is trained to be a really, really good next-token predictor over the empirical distribution of human-written text. Everything the model appears to _know_ (language structure, world facts, programming languages, mathematical reasoning, what a haiku looks like) is encoded in the parameters because predicting the next token well _requires_ a representation that captures all of those things. To predict the next word of a sentence about the French Revolution, the model has to encode something that functions like a representation of the French Revolution. To predict the next character of a Python file with a syntax error, the model has to encode something that functions like an understanding of Python syntax. These representations are not labeled; they emerge from the prediction task. This is the deep insight of the GPT series and the foundation of the whole modern field.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
#### What the engineer needs to take from this

A few things follow that are load-bearing for the rest of this book.

**The model has a knowledge cutoff.** The training data was gathered by some date, and the model knows nothing definitive after that date. (It may have absorbed some signal about events after the cutoff if those events were referenced in later training data, but you cannot rely on it.) Chapter 9 (RAG) is, in a real sense, the discipline of getting the model post-cutoff information by putting it directly into the input sequence.

**The model knows your data only if your data was in its training set.** Your internal company wiki was probably not in the training set. Your proprietary codebase was probably not. The clinical notes at Beacon Health AI were definitely not (PHI is not on the public web). This is the second motivation for RAG.

**The model's behavior reflects the empirical distribution of the training corpus.** The internet is the dominant source. The model has Reddit in it; it has Wikipedia in it; it has bad answers from forum posts in it; it has high-quality textbooks in it. Without further training, the model would generate a statistically weighted average of all of this. This is why pretraining alone is not enough to produce a useful chat product. The next step (RLHF / DPO) is what makes the model preferentially produce the good-textbook style rather than the bad-forum style.

**The model has no concept of _now_.** It does not know what time it is. It does not know which model version it is. It does not know what the price of Anthropic's API is. Things that seem like obvious facts about the world _that depend on the model's runtime context_ must be supplied to it via the prompt. (Try asking the model what year it is. The honest answer is _I do not know; it depends on when you are asking me, and I cannot perceive that_. Many models will guess, often based on cutoff data, and the guess will be wrong.)

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
### 2.3 RLHF and DPO at the engineer's level: turning the base model into a chat model

A pretrained base model is, technically, a finished thing. But it is not a useful chat product. If you ask a pretrained-only model _what is the capital of France?_ , you may get back the correct answer; you may get back another question; you may get back a paragraph beginning _Such trivia questions can be found in any encyclopedia, but…_. The base model is doing what it was trained to do: predicting what tokens are most likely to follow your prompt according to the empirical distribution of text. It is not trying to be helpful, because helpfulness was not the training objective.

To turn a base model into a chat model, you do a second training step. Two main techniques are in use as of 2026:

**RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)** , the original technique from the InstructGPT and ChatGPT line. You collect a smaller dataset of conversations where a human has rated the model's responses (or compared two responses and picked the preferred one). You train a separate reward model to predict the human preference. Then you fine-tune the base model using reinforcement learning to maximize the reward model's predicted score. The result is a model that has learned to produce responses that humans tend to prefer.

**DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)** , a more recent technique that achieves a similar outcome without the separate reward-model step. The model is directly fine-tuned on preference pairs (chosen response vs rejected response) using a contrastive loss. DPO is simpler to implement and is increasingly the default in 2026.

There are variants and competitors (PPO, RLAIF, Constitutional AI). The engineer's-level takeaway is the same regardless of technique: after pretraining, the model goes through a _preference-tuning_ phase that teaches it to behave the way the chat product wants it to behave. The chat persona, the refusal patterns ("I cannot help with that"), the structured-response habits, the disposition to be helpful and harmless: all of these are installed in this second phase.


#### What this means for engineers

A few practical consequences.

**The chat-model behavior is a layer on top of the base model.** The base model still knows everything it learned in pretraining. The preference-tuning sometimes _suppresses_ knowledge (refusing to discuss certain topics) but the knowledge is still in the weights. This is why jailbreaks work: you can sometimes coax the model into bypassing the trained refusal behavior and revealing the underlying base knowledge.

**Different chat models from the same lab can behave noticeably differently.** Anthropic's Claude family, OpenAI's GPT family, Google's Gemini family each get distinct preference-tuning recipes. Even the same lab, across versions (Sonnet 4 vs Sonnet 4.5), changes the behavior. This is why the model upgrade workflow (Chapter 21) is non-trivial: behavior changes, even when the underlying capability is similar.

**Preference-tuning installs the system prompt as a privileged channel.** Modern chat models are trained to follow instructions in the _system_ role more strictly than instructions in the _user_ role. This is the foundation of the _role-based separation_ that Chapter 3 will introduce and Chapter 23 will lean on heavily for prompt-injection defense.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
### 2.4 The context window: what it actually is, and why it matters

Every modern LLM has a _context window_ : the maximum length, in tokens, of the input sequence the model can process in one call. As of 2026, frontier models have context windows from 128K tokens (GPT-4o) to 200K tokens (Claude Sonnet 4 family) to 2M tokens (Gemini 2.5 Pro long-context configuration).

The context window is a hard architectural limit. You cannot exceed it. If your input exceeds the context window, the API either errors out or silently truncates (depending on the provider and the endpoint). Engineering around the context window (what to put in, what to leave out, how to compress, when to switch to retrieval) is the topic of Chapter 8. For now, what matters is what the context window _is_.

The context window is the model's working memory. Within the window, the model can attend to any token. Outside the window, the model has no access. There is no _long-term memory_ baked into the model in the way humans have one; everything the model considers when generating the next token comes from (a) its training, encoded in the weights, and (b) the current input sequence within the context window. If you want the model to remember the conversation from yesterday, you have to put yesterday's conversation back into the input today. If you want the model to know about your internal documents, you have to put the documents back into the input.

This is the foundation of the field of _context engineering_ (Chapter 8), and it is the foundation of RAG (Chapters 9–12), and it is the foundation of agent memory architectures (Chapter 14). The context window is the only place state lives during a single inference call.


#### Why "lost in the middle" is a real phenomenon

A 2023 paper (Liu et al., known informally as the _lost in the middle_ paper) showed that, on retrieval-style tasks where a model is given a long context containing a relevant snippet at some position, the model's accuracy on extracting the right information varies based on _where in the context_ the snippet appears. Information at the beginning of the context, and at the end, is more reliably attended to than information in the middle.

The phenomenon has been ameliorated in newer models (frontier 2024 and 2025 models are noticeably better at long-context retrieval than the 2023-era models the paper studied), but it has not gone away. It is a tendency, not a hard failure, and Chapter 8 will return to it: in 2026, the practical implication is that you should put the most critical instructions at the _end_ of your prompt (closest to where generation begins) and the most critical reference material toward the _start_ and the _end_ of the context, with less-critical material in the middle.

This is the kind of detail that is invisible without inside-the-box knowledge (it would not occur to someone who treats the LLM as a black box) but it is operationally important. You will engineer around it in Chapter 8.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
### 2.5 The generation loop: where stochasticity comes from

Recall the loop from §2.1. The model returns a probability distribution over the next token; you sample from the distribution; you append the sample; you go again. The sampling step is where stochasticity comes from. The distribution is deterministic given a fixed input (modulo a small amount of GPU-level non-determinism in some implementations); the _choice_ of which token to emit is random, weighted by the distribution.

The sampling step is controlled by parameters that the API exposes. These are the levers an engineer turns, and Chapter 3 will exercise them in detail. For now, let's get the mental model right.


#### Definition: Temperature

A scalar parameter (usually in [0.0, 2.0]) controlling the sharpness of the next-token distribution before sampling. At temperature 0, the model deterministically picks the highest-probability token at every step (this is called _greedy decoding_). At temperature 1, the model samples from the raw distribution. At temperature > 1, the distribution is softened, so low-probability tokens become more likely. At temperature < 1 but > 0, the distribution is sharpened, so high-probability tokens become even more likely.

In plain language: temperature is the _creativity knob_. Low temperature is for tasks where you want consistent, reliable, conservative outputs (structured extraction, code generation in production, classification). High temperature is for tasks where you want diversity (brainstorming, creative writing). The default for most production tasks is in the 0.0–0.3 range; many production systems run at literal 0 for reproducibility.

A subtle point that bites in production: even at temperature 0, you may see non-determinism in practice. This is because the GPU-level operations used to compute the distribution are not fully associative under floating-point arithmetic, and slight differences in how the operations are scheduled (e.g., across instance restarts) can change which token has the highest probability when two candidates are very close. The variance is small, but it exists. The right way to think about it: temperature 0 gives you _near-deterministic_ behavior, not strict determinism, and you should not rely on bit-exact reproducibility across calls.


#### Definition: Top-p (nucleus sampling)

A parameter (in [0.0, 1.0]) that limits sampling to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is at least p. Top-p of 0.9 means: at each step, sort the tokens by probability, take the smallest set whose probabilities sum to at least 0.9, renormalize, and sample from that set.

In plain language: top-p is the _truncation_ knob. It clips the long tail of low-probability tokens, preventing the model from emitting a wildly unlikely token just because the distribution had non-zero mass there. The default (top-p ~0.9 to 1.0) is fine for most uses; lowering it (e.g., 0.5) makes outputs more conservative without making them deterministic the way temperature 0 does.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
#### Definition: Top-k

A parameter (positive integer) that limits sampling to the top-k highest-probability tokens at each step. Top-k of 50 means: at each step, take the 50 highest-probability tokens, renormalize, and sample from that set.

Top-k is older than top-p and has largely been replaced by top-p in modern APIs (Anthropic and OpenAI both default to ignoring or omitting top-k). When both are set, the effect is to take the intersection: the top-k highest-probability tokens, further restricted to the top-p mass.


#### The combinatorics of stochasticity

Why care about this? Because _the same prompt produces different outputs across calls_ is a property your product inherits, and your eval discipline has to accommodate. If you run a single prompt 100 times at temperature 0.7, you get 100 different responses. Some will be subtly different (one word changed); some will be substantially different (different reasoning paths, different conclusions). This is not a bug. It is the design.

For an engineer, the implications are:

  1. **Reproducibility requires temperature 0** (modulo the GPU caveat). For debugging, for regression tests, for legal compliance, set temperature to 0 and treat the output as the canonical output for that input.
  2. **Eval suites have to account for variability**. If you score your model's output on a task at temperature 0.7, run the eval N times (typically N=3 to 5) and report the distribution, not a point estimate. Otherwise, a regression detected at one run may be noise.
  3. **Some failure modes are stochastic**. A prompt-injection attack may work 30% of the time. A safety filter may fail 1% of the time. You cannot detect these by spot-checking; you have to measure them at sample sizes large enough to estimate the rate.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
### 2.6 Why LLMs hallucinate: the architectural answer

Hallucination, the model confidently producing factually false information, is the most-discussed failure mode of LLMs. The engineer's-level explanation is straightforward.

Recall the generation loop: at every step, the model picks a next token by sampling from a probability distribution. The model is _always_ picking _something_. It does not have a separate machinery for _I do not know_. When the next-token distribution is sharply peaked on a single token, the model emits a confident-feeling completion. When the next-token distribution is more uniform, because the model genuinely does not have a clear prediction, the model emits _something anyway_ , drawn from the (now less peaked) distribution. To an outside reader, the resulting text looks just as confident as a peaked-distribution completion. The model's words do not carry probability information.

So: hallucinations are the visible artifact of the model having to commit to a next-token choice even when its uncertainty is high. The model does not know it does not know. The model just emits the most-likely token in its distribution, and if the most-likely token in a high-uncertainty distribution is a plausible-sounding but wrong piece of information, you get a hallucination.

A few corollaries follow.

**Hallucinations are not random.** They tend to occur in regions of "factual" output (names, dates, citations, numerical figures) more than in stylistic output. If the model is producing prose about an abstract topic, it is generating stylistic continuations that do not strongly require factual grounding; the uncertainty is well-handled. If the model is producing a citation to a specific paper, it is committing to a sequence of tokens (author name, year, title) where any wrong token produces a wrong citation, and the model's training has many plausible patterns to interpolate from. This is why "hallucinated citations" are the canonical hallucination example.

**Hallucinations are not the same as lying.** The model is not deceiving you; it is producing the most-likely token according to its training, with no introspective access to the fact that it is producing something unreliable. _Lying_ implies an awareness of truth that is being violated; the model has no such awareness. This is a useful frame because it removes the moral language and clarifies the engineering problem: we are dealing with a system that emits outputs at calibrated levels of probability, and the calibration is imperfect.

**Hallucinations are mitigated, not eliminated, by post-training.** RLHF/DPO can teach the model patterns like "I do not have information about that" when it detects certain kinds of out-of-distribution queries. But the model cannot reliably introspect on its own uncertainty. It cannot say _I am 60% sure about this_ ; it can only say _I am sure_ or _I am not sure_ , and the choice between those framings is itself a trained behavior, not a true uncertainty estimate. Chapter 23 will engage with this directly under the heading of _confidence calibration_.

**Hallucinations are the deepest motivation for RAG.** If the model's uncertainty about a fact is the source of hallucination, putting the fact directly into the input sequence eliminates the uncertainty. RAG is, in a sense, a way of forcing the model into low-uncertainty next-token predictions by supplying the relevant facts in its context. Chapter 9 will build this out.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

Hallucinations cannot be prompted away. "Tell the model not to hallucinate, and it won't" is a tempting but unreliable belief. The model does not have a _do not hallucinate_ switch. You can sometimes reduce the rate of hallucination by prompting the model to express uncertainty ("if you do not know, say you do not know"), but the model's compliance with this instruction is itself trained behavior, and it varies with the prompt and the topic. The reliable mitigations for hallucination are _architectural_ : ground the model in retrieved facts (RAG), structure the output (force JSON schema so the model has to commit to specific fields with validation), give the model tools to look things up (Chapter 13), and design the system to refuse gracefully when confidence is low (Chapter 23). Prompt-only hallucination control is not engineering-grade.


### 2.7 Why LLMs are prompt-sensitive

A small change to the wording of a prompt can produce a noticeably different output. This is jarring to engineers used to deterministic interfaces. The explanation is straightforward at the architectural level.

The model's next-token distribution is computed by attending to every token in the input sequence with a learned attention mechanism. Different tokens influence the distribution differently. When you change a prompt (say, replacing _please summarize this_ with _summarize the following_) you are changing the input sequence, and the model's attention patterns over that sequence will be different. The downstream effect on the output can be larger than the surface change in the prompt would suggest.

This is _not a bug_. It is the model behaving as designed. The model is not parsing your prompt into a semantic intent and then acting on the intent; it is computing a distribution over next tokens conditioned on the specific tokens you supplied. The intent is implicit in the tokens, and changing the tokens changes the conditioning.

A few practical consequences:

**Prompts are versioned artifacts.** If a prompt is in your production system, it is code, and it deserves the same version control, code review, and regression testing as any other production code. Chapter 6 will turn this into the prompt-registry pattern.

**Prompt changes need eval regression checks.** A prompt change can subtly degrade output quality without any obvious user-visible symptom. The only reliable detection is an eval suite. Chapter 5 builds the workflow.

**Few-shot examples matter.** Showing the model 2–5 examples of what you want (in the prompt) often produces a larger behavior change than detailed natural-language instructions. The model can pattern-match on examples more reliably than it can interpret abstract instructions. Chapter 6 will build out the technique.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
### 2.8 Why LLMs cannot reliably count letters

This is a classic question in _what is the model good at and bad at_. If you ask Claude or GPT-4o _how many r's are in the word strawberry?_ , you may get the right answer or you may not. This is not a flaw in a single model; it is a consequence of tokenization.

Recall from §2.1 that the model never sees text. It sees integer tokens. The word _strawberry_ is, in many tokenizers, a single token, so the model receives one integer. To answer _how many r's are in this token?_ , the model would have to do something that does not naturally fall out of its architecture: it would have to introspect on the _spelling_ of a token whose internal structure the model does not directly process. The model can sometimes do this, by drawing on training data that talks about the spelling of words, but it is unreliable. The model's strong suits are pattern completion over sequences of tokens; the model's weak suits are operations that require character-level access to those tokens.

This generalizes. LLMs are unreliable at:

* Counting characters in a word
* Counting words in a sentence
* Determining the position of a substring (third character of a token, etc.)
* Reversing a word
* Anagrams
* Arithmetic with many digits (modern tokenizers actually split digits one per token to help — but the transformer architecture still lacks dedicated carry-propagation circuitry, and its limited depth means multi-step arithmetic exceeds what the model can reliably do in a single forward pass)
* Counting items in a list, especially long lists

The mitigation for an engineer is _do not ask the model to do tasks that require character-level access to tokens_. If you need to count characters, do it in code outside the model. If you need to do arithmetic, give the model a calculator tool (Chapter 13). If you need to reverse a string, do it in code. The model is good at high-level reasoning over sequences; the model is bad at character-level mechanics. Knowing the difference is mental-model work.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
### 2.9 The model card as a spec sheet

Every frontier model release in 2026 comes with a _model card_ : a document published by the lab describing the model's capabilities, limitations, intended use, evaluation results on standard benchmarks, safety testing results, and operational characteristics (context window, supported features, pricing). The model card is the spec sheet for the model, and an engineer should read it the way a chip engineer reads a datasheet.

What to look for in a 2026 model card, as an AI engineer:

  1. **Context window** (in tokens, separately for input and possibly output)
  2. **Knowledge cutoff** (the date past which the model has no reliable training data)
  3. **Supported features** : streaming, tool use, JSON-schema output, vision, audio in/out, long-context billing rates
  4. **Pricing** : input cost per million tokens, output cost per million tokens, any per-feature surcharges (vision is often higher than text, batch is often 50% off)
  5. **Benchmark results** : MMLU, HumanEval, AIME, etc. (useful as relative comparison between models, not as absolute capability statements)
  6. **Safety evaluation** : refusal rates, prompt-injection susceptibility, red-team results
  7. **Latency characteristics** : time to first token, output tokens per second, often broken out by region and traffic level
  8. **Rate limits** : requests per minute and tokens per minute by default; what tiers unlock higher limits
  9. **Deprecation timeline** (if disclosed): when the model is expected to be sunset, and what its successor is

Two notes on the limits of model cards. First, lab-reported benchmark numbers are marketing-adjacent: they tend to be the model's best performance on the chosen benchmarks, and they do not generalize to your task. Always run your own evals. Second, model cards are documents about capabilities, not contracts about behavior: the model's behavior on your specific prompts is empirical, not deducible from the card. The card narrows the search space; it does not replace eval.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
### 2.10 Triangle Trade-off sidebar: cost-breakdown of a single API call

The mental model from §2.1–§2.9 leaves one practical question to put a number on: when you call the model, what are you actually paying for? The cost shape is itself a property of the mental model — cost is denominated in _tokens_ , the same units the model reasons over, and the input/output asymmetry in pricing has a mechanistic reason rooted in how the model generates (every output token requires a full forward pass, every input token does not). This sidebar makes the connection concrete; Chapter 3 operationalizes it at the API layer; Chapter 18 turns it into the cost-engineering discipline. Let's trace a single Sonnet 4 call from the perspective of cost.

A typical chat-API call to Sonnet 4 in 2026 has the following cost components, all denominated in tokens:

* **System prompt** : usually 300–1500 tokens. At 3 USD per million input tokens, this is 0.0009 USD to 0.0045 USD per call. _Cached after the first call within the 5-minute TTL window (Chapter 18); the cached read rate is 0.30 USD per million tokens, or about 0.0001 USD to 0.0005 USD per call._
* **User message and conversation history** : highly variable. A new conversation has just the user message (maybe 50–500 tokens, 0.00015 USD to 0.0015 USD). A 20-turn conversation can be 5K–20K tokens cumulative (0.015 USD to 0.06 USD in input).
* **Retrieved RAG context (if applicable)** : 1K–10K tokens added per retrieval. At 3 USD per million input, that is 0.003 USD to 0.03 USD per call.
* **Tool definitions (if applicable)** : 200–1500 tokens. Same per-token cost as system prompt; cached the same way.
* **Model response (output)** : 100–2000 tokens typical for chat; can be much longer for code generation or document synthesis. At 15 USD per million output tokens, that is 0.0015 USD to 0.03 USD per call. _Note the 5× ratio of output to input cost: this is true across most provider pricing in 2026, and it means that whenever you can structure a task to reduce output length without hurting quality, you save real money._

Pulling these together for a representative production scenario: a customer-support agent at Helios making a single tool-augmented response with a 1500-token system prompt (cached), 500 tokens of recent conversation history, 2K tokens of retrieved knowledge-base context, 800 tokens of tool definitions (cached), and 600 tokens of model response. The cost decomposition:

* System prompt (cached read): 1500 × 0.30 USD / 1M = **0.00045 USD**
* Conversation history (fresh input): 500 × 3.00 USD / 1M = **0.0015 USD**
* Retrieved context (fresh input): 2000 × 3.00 USD / 1M = **0.006 USD**
* Tool definitions (cached read): 800 × 0.30 USD / 1M = **0.00024 USD**
* Output: 600 × 15.00 USD / 1M = **0.009 USD**
* **Total per call: ~0.017 USD (rounded up to 0.02 USD to leave headroom for variance and longer outputs)**

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
At Helios's 10 million tickets per month, with an average of 4 model calls per ticket (one for understanding, one for retrieval-augmented response, one for tool invocation, one for follow-up), that is 40 million calls per month — about **680K USD/month** at the unit cost of 0.017, USD or **~800K USD/month** at the 0.02 USD rounded-up unit cost. Both lower-bound estimates are close to Helios's reported 1M USD+ monthly inference spend. The gap to the reported figure is covered by occasional much-longer responses, multi-call ticket flows that overrun the four-call average, and occasional routing to a more expensive frontier model (Opus-class) for sensitive escalations where Sonnet's quality is not enough.

Two things to notice in this breakdown:

  1. **The output is the dominant cost line per call** , even though it is one of the smaller token counts. The 5× output-vs-input pricing multiplier means a 600-token output costs more than a 2000-token input. This is why prompt design that yields shorter, more structured outputs (Chapter 7) is a real cost lever, not just a quality concern.
  2. **Prompt caching is a big lever when it applies**. The system prompt and the tool definitions, both cached, cost 10× less per call than they would uncached. For a high-volume system where system prompts and tool definitions are stable, prompt caching can reduce per-call cost by 30–60%. Chapter 18 will turn this into binding workflow #9.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
### 2.11 How This Breaks: confusing the model with the product

**Failure mode named** : confusing the model with the product. A team treats the LLM as if it were the product, rather than as a probabilistic component inside the product. Behavior that needs to be guaranteed (refusal on certain topics, specific output formats, attribution of sources, escalation paths) is delegated entirely to the model's trained behavior, with no enforcement layer outside the model.

**Real or composite incident** : a composite example from across the industry. A startup ships an LLM-backed customer service feature that, per the system prompt, _should_ refuse to make commitments on the company's behalf: pricing, refunds, policy exceptions. The system prompt says so in three places, with examples. Six weeks after launch, a user constructs a prompt that exploits a quirk of how the model interprets nested instructions, and the model emits a commitment ("yes, we will refund you 500 USD for the inconvenience"). The user takes a screenshot. The legal team gets involved.

The failure was not that the model is bad. The failure was that _the engineering team treated the system prompt as a guarantee, when in fact the system prompt is a probabilistic conditioner that biases the model's behavior but does not enforce it_. There was no output-validation layer. There was no refusal classifier on the output. There was no tool-call mediation that would have routed any _refund commitment_ through a deterministic policy check.

**Engineering mitigation** : separate the _model_ from the _product_. The system prompt does its job (biasing the model's behavior). A separate output-validation layer enforces the hard constraints: it runs a refusal classifier, checks for committed dollar amounts above a threshold, and validates the response shape. For agent-style flows with tool calls, the deterministic policy check happens at the tool layer, not in the model's natural language. The model is a component; the product is what you wrap around the component. Chapter 16 will build this principle into a 9-layer reference architecture. Chapter 23 will return to it under the heading of _safety in production_.

**The eval that would have caught it** : a _prompt-injection robustness_ eval. A golden set of 100+ adversarial inputs designed to elicit refusal-violations from the model. Run on every prompt change and every model upgrade. If the system prompt is the only line of defense, an adversarial eval at this scale will surface the gaps within a day. If the output-validation layer is in place, the eval should show a robust 0% refusal-violation rate even when the model itself is occasionally tricked, because the validation layer catches what the model misses. The presence of the eval is what would have caught it; the failure is that no such eval existed before launch.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

An LLM is, mechanically, a function that turns a sequence of tokens into a probability distribution over the next token. Everything else (the chat product, the agent, the RAG system, the voice assistant) is engineering wrapped around that one function. Tokens are integer-encoded units of input and output; the model never sees text. Pretraining gave the model its knowledge of language and the world by training on enormous corpora to predict the next token; preference tuning (RLHF, DPO) turned the base model into a helpful, instruction-following chat model. The context window is the model's working memory and the only place state lives during a single inference call. Hallucinations are the visible artifact of the model having to commit to a next-token choice even under high uncertainty. Prompt sensitivity comes from the fact that the model is conditioning on specific tokens, not parsing an abstract intent. The model cannot reliably count letters because it never sees them; tokenization sits between text and the model. The model card is the spec sheet; treat it that way.

The three teams from Chapter 1 will keep showing up; Chapter 3 will hand you the API surface that makes this mental model concrete. Almost every chapter that follows leans on the model built here. Context engineering (Chapter 8) builds on §2.4; RAG (Chapter 9) is the architectural answer to §2.6; tool use (Chapter 13) is the engineering answer to §2.8; cost optimization (Chapter 18) is the engineering answer to §2.10. The four-question rubric and the _How This Breaks_ pattern recur throughout, and each recurrence rests on what you internalized here.

The most important thing to carry into Chapter 3 is the loop: _given a sequence of tokens, the model returns a probability distribution over the next token, you sample, you append, you repeat until stop._ If that loop is in your head, the API surface in Chapter 3 will make immediate sense, and the whole book will compound.


### 2.X Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** A junior engineer says: "I'll set temperature to 0 so that my eval suite is fully reproducible across runs." What two caveats would you add to this plan, and how would you mitigate them?

Hint

One caveat is about the model's behavior at exactly temperature 0. The other is about what _reproducible_ means across versions of the underlying infrastructure.

**Answer:** Two caveats:

  1. **Temperature 0 is near-deterministic, not strictly deterministic.** GPU-level non-associativity in floating-point operations can cause the model to occasionally pick a different highest-probability token when two candidates are very close. The mitigation is to run the eval multiple times (say, N=3) at temperature 0 and verify that the outputs match in nearly every case; treat the rare divergences as expected and either report a small variance budget or use a comparison metric that tolerates token-level swaps that do not change the semantic content.

  2. **Model versions change underneath you.** A provider can release a minor update to Sonnet 4 (say, from Sonnet 4 to Sonnet 4-2026-04-15) without renaming the model in your API call. Your "reproducible" eval can produce different results on different days if you do not pin to a specific dated model version. The mitigation is to pin to dated model versions explicitly in your eval configuration, treat any change in model version as a release event that triggers a full eval re-run, and snapshot the dated version in your version-control alongside the prompt. Chapter 21 turns this into the full model upgrade workflow.

The plan to set temperature to 0 is necessary but not sufficient. Add: (a) multi-run averaging at the eval level; (b) explicit model-version pinning; (c) treat eval as a function of (prompt, model version, system context) and version-control all three.

**Q2.** A teammate explains that the model "knows" something because it answered correctly when asked. Reframe this in terms of the mental model from §2.1–2.3. What is actually going on, and what implications does it have for whether you should rely on that knowledge in production?

**Answer:** The teammate's framing is the _knowledge as retrieval_ misconception. What actually happened is that the model emitted a sequence of tokens that constituted a correct answer because the next-token distributions, conditioned on the question, were sharply peaked on tokens that spelled out the right answer. This is _not_ the same as the model having a verified database of facts that it queried. The model's "knowledge" is statistical: it is whatever the training corpus reinforced enough to produce sharp predictions on related queries.

Three implications for production reliance:

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
1. **Confidence is not calibrated.** The model emits the correct answer with high _visible_ confidence, but it also emits incorrect answers with the same visible confidence (this is the hallucination phenomenon, §2.6). The fact that the model answered correctly once does not mean it will answer correctly the next time on a slightly different phrasing.
  2. **Knowledge cutoff matters.** If the question's answer depends on information after the training cutoff, the model is producing a guess regardless of how confident it sounds. You cannot tell from the model's output whether it is operating on solid training data or extrapolating.
  3. **The answer should be grounded if it matters.** For any production use where being right matters, supply the relevant fact in the input (via RAG or via a tool call) rather than relying on the model's training-encoded knowledge. The model is much better at _answering questions when given the relevant context_ than at _recalling facts from training_. Chapter 9 (RAG) is the engineering version of this principle.

So: the model did not _know_ anything; it produced an output that was correct because its training was good in that region. The implication is _do not bet a production system on that being reliable_.

**Q3.** Tokenization causes a class of failures in which the model cannot reliably perform character-level operations (counting letters, reversing strings, manipulating substrings). For each of the following tasks, decide whether the model can be relied on, or whether you should pre-process or post-process in code:

* (a) Counting the number of items in a comma-separated list provided in the prompt
* (b) Producing a slugified version of a user's submitted blog-post title
* (c) Extracting the URL from a sentence the user wrote
* (d) Generating SQL from a natural-language question

**Answer:**

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
* **(a) Counting CSV items** : do not rely on the model. The model is bad at counting, especially when the count is the primary requested operation. Do the count in code: split the string on commas (handling escaped commas if relevant) and take the length. The model can be useful for _understanding_ a list, but not for _counting_ it.
* **(b) Slugifying** : do not rely on the model for the canonical slug. Use a code library (e.g., Python's `python-slugify`). The model will produce reasonable slugs for English text but is inconsistent on edge cases (Unicode, very long titles, titles with mostly punctuation) where a library will be reliable. If you really want LLM involvement, use it to _propose_ a slug that a deterministic post-processor then normalizes.
* **(c) URL extraction** : this one is borderline. The model can extract URLs from short prose reasonably well. For production reliability, especially when URLs may be malformed or embedded in unusual ways, prefer a regex (or a parser library) to extract candidate URLs, and only use the model if the task is _which of these URLs is most relevant to the user's intent?_ , a judgment task the model handles well.
* **(d) SQL generation** : this is the model's strong suit, not its weak suit. Generating SQL from natural language is a task the model has seen abundantly in training and is good at, _as long as you give it the schema_. Provide the table definitions in the prompt. The model can produce useful SQL; in production, you may want to add a validator (parse the SQL, check that it does not contain unsafe operations like dropping tables, restrict to read-only). The model is the right tool for the high-level task; code is the right tool for safety post-processing.

The general principle: use the model for tasks that involve _understanding semantics_ or _generating fluent text_ ; use code for tasks that involve _exact mechanics on bytes/characters_ ; combine them when both are needed. Chapter 13 will formalize this with tool use.

**Q4.** Why are prompt-injection attacks "more architectural than fixable by prompting"? Refer to the mental model in §2.3 and §2.7 in your answer.

**Answer:** Prompt-injection attacks exploit the fact that, at the architectural level, the model conditions on the entire input sequence and computes next-token distributions accordingly. There is no internal mechanism that separates "trusted instructions from the developer's system prompt" from "untrusted content from a user message or a retrieved document." The privileged-channel status of the system role is a _trained behavior_ installed during RLHF/DPO (§2.3): the model has been shown many examples where it should prefer system-role instructions over conflicting user-role instructions, so it tends to do so. But this preference is statistical, not architectural. A sufficiently clever user message or a piece of injected content in a retrieved document can shift the model's next-token distributions enough to override the trained preference.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
You cannot fix this with prompting. Any "prompt-engineering" defense (telling the model in its system prompt to ignore injection attempts) is itself just another condition the model is balancing against the injected content. Some defenses help on average; none are airtight. The right mitigations are architectural (§2.11's _separate the model from the product_ ; Chapter 23's four-layer defense): treat the model's output as untrusted; validate it before acting on it; isolate tool calls behind deterministic policy checks; tag untrusted content in the input so the model treats it as data, not as instruction. These are engineering layers around the model, not prompts to the model.

The chapter's emphasis on prompt-sensitivity (§2.7) and on the absence of an internal _do not hallucinate_ switch (§2.6) generalizes: there is no internal _do not be tricked_ switch either. The model is a probabilistic conditioner; the only reliable defenses are layered around it.

**Q5.** Prompt caching (0.30 USD/1M cached read vs 3.00 USD/1M fresh input on Sonnet 4) is the engineering-visible artifact of the KV cache, an internal mechanism inside the model's serving stack. Explain, at the engineer's level, what the KV cache actually is and why a 10× price discount on cached input is economically defensible for the provider rather than a marketing promotion. Then identify one prompt design decision that this fact should change.

Hint

The K and V stand for _key_ and _value_ , two of the three matrices computed for every token at every layer during the transformer's attention step. Which of those matrices depends only on previously-seen tokens, and which depends on the new token?

**Answer:** At the engineer's level: when the model processes a prompt, every token at every transformer layer produces three projected vectors called the query, key, and value. The attention mechanism uses queries against keys to decide _which earlier tokens to attend to_ , and the resulting attention scores are applied to the values. The key and value matrices for tokens 1 through N depend only on those tokens; once computed, they can be cached and reused if the same prefix is sent again. Only the new query has to be computed against the existing keys when extending the prompt with new tokens. This is the KV cache: it is the model's serving-stack memoization of (key, value) tensors for prompt prefixes that have been seen before.

The 10× discount is defensible because the provider's actual marginal cost on a cache hit is dominated by the value-application and softmax step over the cached keys, not by the much more expensive forward pass that would have computed those keys from scratch. The compute work saved is a large fraction of the prompt-encoding cost. Providers price the discount conservatively (they could in principle price cached reads even cheaper) because cache hits are not guaranteed across requests and the infrastructure for prefix-matching has its own overhead. The point is: this is real compute being saved, not a sales gimmick.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src: One prompt design decision this changes: **put the long, stable, system-level material at the _front_ of the prompt and the short, per-request material at the _back_**. Reverse that order and you waste your cache, because the cache matches on prefixes. Specifically: system prompt, then few-shot examples, then long retrieved context, then the user's query last. This is the canonical layout, and the KV-cache explanation is why it is the canonical layout rather than an arbitrary stylistic preference. Chapter 8 will return to this when it formalizes context engineering.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** _Estimating the cost of a feature_. You are scoping a chat feature for the Beacon Health CodeReview Bot. The feature will:

* Use a fixed 1200-token system prompt (cached, 0.30 USD/1M effective)
* Include the diff being reviewed (typical: 2500 tokens, fresh input)
* Have no retrieved RAG context (the model uses the diff directly)
* Use no tools
* Produce structured-output reviews of approximately 800 tokens

Estimate the per-PR inference cost at Sonnet 4 (3.00 USD/1M input fresh, 0.30 USD/1M cached read, 15.00 USD/1M output). The team handles 80 PRs per day across the engineering org. Estimate the monthly inference cost. Also estimate what the cost would be at GPT-4o-mini (0.15 USD/1M input, 0.60 USD/1M output) and at Claude Haiku (0.80 USD/1M input, 4 USD/1M output), both reasonable cheaper alternatives.

Hint

Compute the per-call cost as the sum of (input tokens × input rate) + (output tokens × output rate), being careful to use the cached-read rate for the cacheable portion.

**Answer:** Per-PR cost decomposition at Sonnet 4:

* System prompt (cached read): 1200 × 0.30 USD/1M = **0.00036 USD**
* Diff (fresh input): 2500 × 3.00 USD/1M = **0.0075 USD**
* Output: 800 × 15.00 USD/1M = **0.012 USD**
* **Total per PR: ~0.0199 USD ≈ 0.020 USD**

At 80 PRs/day × 30 days = 2400 PRs/month: **2400 × 0.020 USD = 48 USD/month** at Sonnet 4.

At GPT-4o-mini:

* System prompt: 1200 × 0.15 USD/1M = 0.00018 USD (mini does not have the same prompt-caching discount as Sonnet; treat as fresh)
* Diff: 2500 × 0.15 USD/1M = 0.000375 USD
* Output: 800 × 0.60 USD/1M = 0.00048 USD
* **Per PR: ~0.001 USD**
* **Monthly: 2400 × 0.001 USD = 2.40 USD/month** at GPT-4o-mini

At Claude Haiku:

* System prompt: 1200 × 0.80 USD/1M = 0.00096 USD (Haiku also offers prompt caching; if available, the cached rate would be ~0.08 USD/1M, dropping system prompt to ~0.0001. USD For this estimate, use fresh.)
* Diff: 2500 × 0.80 USD/1M = 0.002 USD
* Output: 800 × 4.00 USD/1M = 0.0032 USD
* **Per PR: ~0.006 USD**
* **Monthly: 2400 × 0.006 USD = 14.40 USD/month** at Haiku

The cheapest option is ~20× cheaper than the most expensive. At this scale (48 USD/month vs 2.40 USD/month), the absolute saving is small enough that you should pick on quality, not cost, since the cost is a rounding error in the engineer's salary. The decision-relevant question is whether GPT-4o-mini produces good enough reviews on your eval set; if yes, use it; if not, pay the extra 46 USD/month for Sonnet 4. Chapter 17 (multi-model routing) will let you mix-and-match: use the cheap model for easy reviews, escalate to Sonnet 4 for PRs that touch sensitive code paths.

**AI-collaboration sub-question** : How would you ask an LLM to help with this exercise, and what would you verify in its response?

**Answer:** Useful prompt: _I am estimating LLM inference costs for a feature that handles 80 PRs/day with a 1200-token cached system prompt, 2500-token fresh input, and 800-token output. Give me a per-PR cost calculation at Anthropic's current 2026 prices for Sonnet 4, Haiku, and OpenAI's GPT-4o-mini._ You verify by (a) checking that the LLM's quoted prices match the providers' current public pricing pages (LLMs can hallucinate prices, so always verify), and (b) re-running the arithmetic by hand or in a calculator; the LLM is bad at multi-step arithmetic (§2.8), so do not trust its computed totals without verification.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
**Q2.** _Reading a model card_. Pick any 2026 frontier model you have access to (Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, etc.). Find its model card or product documentation. Extract the following nine values per §2.9: context window, knowledge cutoff, supported features, pricing, benchmark results, safety evaluation, latency characteristics, rate limits, deprecation timeline (if disclosed). For each value, note whether it is _directly stated_ on the model card or _inferred_.

**Answer:** A worked example for Claude Sonnet 4 (your answer should be from a current model card; the numbers here are representative as of 2026 and will date):

Value | Stated or inferred | Note  
---|---|---  
Context window | Stated | 200K tokens input; some configurations offer 1M for long-context premium  
Knowledge cutoff | Stated | Specific month/year  
Features | Stated | Streaming, tool use, vision, JSON-schema output, prompt caching  
Pricing | Stated | 3.00 USD/1M input fresh; 0.30 USD/1M cached read; 15.00 USD/1M output; vision and long-context surcharges separately disclosed  
Benchmarks | Stated | MMLU, HumanEval, MATH, GPQA (provider's reported scores)  
Safety evaluation | Stated | Refusal-rate evaluations; red-team summary; some jailbreak-resistance numbers  
Latency | Partially stated | TTFT (time to first token) p50 typically quoted; throughput sometimes  
Rate limits | Stated | Tier-based; default tier rate limits public, higher tiers via account upgrade  
Deprecation | Sometimes stated | Anthropic publishes deprecation policy generally; specific timelines for prior models are stated  
  
For your actual answer, do this on a model card you have today; the values will change. The exercise is to develop the _habit_ of reading model cards as spec sheets, not as marketing material. When the values are not stated, infer them from API documentation, pricing pages, and your own production measurements.

**AI-collaboration sub-question** : How would you ask an LLM to help with this exercise, and what would you verify in its response?

**Answer:** Useful prompt: _I am building a spec-sheet summary of Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4 model card. List the nine attributes (context window, knowledge cutoff, supported features, pricing, benchmark results, safety evaluation, latency characteristics, rate limits, deprecation timeline) with current 2026 values, and cite the section of the model card or pricing page where each appears._ You verify by cross-checking against the actual current pricing page and model card (LLMs hallucinate model-card details, especially specific benchmark numbers and version-specific feature flags). The LLM is useful for _structuring the summary_ ; you must verify the specific numbers.

**Q3.** _Designing for tokenization-limited tasks_. The Beacon Health CodeReview Bot has to flag PRs that change Python files containing the literal string `# TODO:` more than 5 times. A junior engineer proposes prompting the model: "Look at this diff and tell me whether it adds more than 5 TODO comments." Critique this design and propose an alternative.

Hint

This is exactly the kind of task §2.8 warns about. The model is bad at counting. Where should the counting actually happen?

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
**Answer:** The junior engineer's design has the model doing exactly the wrong job for its architecture. Counting specific substrings in a long diff is a character-level mechanical task that the model is unreliable at: it cannot directly count tokens or substrings, and even when it tries, it may miscount, especially across long inputs.

The right design is to do the counting deterministically in code, and to have the model do the part it is good at:

  1. **Code-level counting** : parse the diff, search for the literal string `# TODO:` in added lines (typically lines starting with `+` in the diff), count the occurrences. This takes ten lines of Python.
  2. **Model-level explanation** : if the count exceeds 5, _then_ invoke the model: give it the offending TODO comments and ask it to summarize whether they look like legitimate work-in-progress markers or like the developer accumulating debt. This is the kind of judgment task the model is good at.

The architectural principle is: **do the deterministic work in code, and reserve the model for tasks that need judgment over semantics**. The model is a probabilistic component; spending its budget on tasks that code can do reliably is wasteful and unreliable. Chapter 13 will turn this into the _tools_ pattern: counting becomes a deterministic tool the model can invoke, with the model orchestrating but not performing the counting.

**AI-collaboration sub-question** : How would you ask an LLM to help with this exercise, and what would you verify in its response?

**Answer:** Useful prompt: _Critique this design: "have the LLM count occurrences of a specific string in a long diff." Suggest a better division of labor between LLM and deterministic code._ The LLM will likely produce a reasonable answer along the lines of "do the counting in code; use the LLM for judgment." You verify by checking that the proposed deterministic counting actually handles the edge cases of your diff format (multi-line comments, strings that contain TODO as a substring, etc.); the LLM's suggestion may gloss over implementation details, and you have to fill those in.

**Q4.** _The hallucination diagnostic_. Your team has noticed that the model occasionally produces an incorrect citation in its outputs, such as a paper title that does not exist attributed to a real author. The team is debating whether to (a) sharpen the prompt to discourage citations, (b) add a post-processor that verifies citations against a list, (c) switch to a different model. Use the mental model from §2.6 to argue for the best approach (or a combination).

Hint

Hallucinations are not prompt-fixable. The choice is between _prevent the model from being in a position to hallucinate_ and _catch hallucinations after the fact_.

**Answer:** The mental model says hallucinations are an artifact of the model committing to next-token outputs even under high uncertainty, especially in factual-citation territory. Prompting alone (option a) can reduce the rate but cannot eliminate it; the model's compliance with "do not cite anything you are not sure about" is itself trained behavior that varies in reliability. So option (a) is a small help, not a solution.

Option (c), switching models, is a band-aid. Different models hallucinate at different rates on different tasks, but no 2026 frontier model is hallucination-free on citation tasks. Switching may shift the failure mode without eliminating it.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
Option (b), the post-processor, is the architectural answer. The post-processor takes the model's output, extracts the cited references, and verifies them against a deterministic source: a database of known papers, a CrossRef DOI lookup, or your own internal knowledge base. References that do not verify are flagged or removed before the output reaches the user. This is the right answer because it converts a probabilistic problem (the model may hallucinate) into a deterministic problem (does this cited reference exist?).

The best engineering choice is **(b) + (a)** : sharpen the prompt to reduce the rate (free win, even if small) and add the post-processor to catch what slips through (the real defense). Combine this with (c) only if your evals show a different model materially reduces the rate; otherwise, the engineering effort is better spent on the post-processor.

For Beacon Health AI specifically, the principle applies with extra weight: a clinical-notes summarizer that hallucinates a medication dose or a diagnosis is catastrophic. The post-processor pattern (treat the model's output as untrusted; validate before showing to the clinician; flag low-confidence outputs for human review) is the design that survives §2.11's _confusing the model with the product_ failure mode.

**AI-collaboration sub-question** : How would you ask an LLM to help with this exercise, and what would you verify in its response?

**Answer:** Useful prompt: _I have an LLM-based system that occasionally hallucinates citations. Walk me through the architecture for a post-processor that verifies citations against CrossRef, what to do when a citation does not verify, and how to design the user-facing output for the verified and unverified cases._ You verify by checking that the proposed CrossRef API usage matches the actual current CrossRef API (LLMs hallucinate API details, especially for less-mainstream APIs), and by sanity-checking the user-facing flow (does _flag and remove_ hide useful context, or is _show with a warning_ better for your users?).

**Q5.** _Engineering a prompt-cache-friendly layout for a real feature_. Strata Research is building a legal-document Q&A surface. Each query carries: a 600-token system prompt that defines the lawyer-persona, an 1800-token "house style guide" the firm wants enforced, ~4000 tokens of retrieved case-law context (different per query), and a ~200-token user question. Currently the team is assembling the prompt as: `[user_question] + [retrieved_context] + [house_style] + [system_prompt]` because "the user question feels most important and should come first." Re-design the layout to maximize prompt-cache hits, estimate the cost savings at 10,000 queries per day on Sonnet 4 (3.00 USD/1M fresh, 0.30 USD/1M cached read), and identify one risk the redesign introduces that the team should eval for.

Hint

The cache matches on prefix. Order the components from most-stable-across-queries to most-variable. Then ask which component is variable but still relatively large.

**Answer:** The current layout is exactly backwards from a cache-utilization standpoint: the most variable component (`user_question`) is at the front, so no prefix is reusable across queries. Almost every token is paid at the fresh rate.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
The re-designed layout, from most-stable to most-variable: `[system_prompt (600)] + [house_style (1800)] + [retrieved_context (4000)] + [user_question (200)]`. The system prompt and house style guide are identical across queries; that is 2400 tokens of cacheable prefix per query. The retrieved context varies per query and will not cache. The user question is small and at the tail.

Cost per query, current layout (no cache):

* All input: (600 + 1800 + 4000 + 200) = 6600 tokens at 3.00 USD/1M = 0.0198 USD
* Plus output (assume 800 tokens at 15.00 USD/1M) = 0.012 USD
* Total per query: ~0.0318 USD
* 10,000/day: 318 USD/day, ~9,540 USD/month

Cost per query, re-designed layout (cache hit on first 2400 tokens):

* Cached prefix: 2400 × 0.30 USD/1M = 0.00072 USD
* Fresh input: (4000 + 200) × 3.00 USD/1M = 0.0126 USD
* Output: 800 × 15.00 USD/1M = 0.012 USD
* Total per query: ~0.0253 USD
* 10,000/day: 253 USD/day, ~7,590 USD/month

Monthly savings: ~1,950, USD or about 20% of the bill. The savings would be much larger if the retrieved context were also cacheable, but it is per-query, so it stays fresh. For cases where the same document is queried multiple times (e.g., a lawyer working on a single case all day), a second-level cache keyed on `(system_prompt + house_style + retrieved_context)` would capture another large fraction; that is the kind of optimization Chapter 18 will formalize.

Risk the team should eval for: **the user question, by being at the _end_ of a 6600-token prompt, may be subject to the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon (§2.4) in reverse — the model may anchor on the retrieved context and answer a question slightly different from the one asked**. The eval is to compare answer quality between the two layouts on a fixed golden set; if quality regresses, the team needs to add explicit "the user's actual question is:" framing immediately before the question, or move the question back to a position the model attends to reliably, even at some cache cost.

**AI-collaboration sub-question** : How would you ask an LLM to help with this exercise, and what would you verify in its response?

**Answer:** Useful prompt: _Here is my current prompt layout for a legal-Q &A feature with components of sizes [600, 1800, 4000, 200] tokens. Propose a layout that maximizes prompt-cache hits on Sonnet 4, compute the per-query cost at 10K queries/day at current Anthropic pricing, and identify the quality risk introduced by the layout change._ You verify by re-running the arithmetic by hand or in a spreadsheet (LLM arithmetic is unreliable per §2.8); by checking the prompt-cache pricing on Anthropic's current docs page; and by stress-testing the proposed quality-risk eval design — would it actually catch a regression where the user question is being misread? If the LLM proposes "compare answer quality between layouts," ask it to specify the metric and the golden-set size and the regression threshold; vague eval design is the most common LLM-suggestion failure.

**Q6.** _Applying Chapter 1's four-question rubric to the hallucination defense_. Chapter 1 (§1.6) introduced the four-question rubric (pattern, eval, failure mode, cost). Apply it explicitly to the post-processor pattern from Q4 above (verify citations against a deterministic source). Write the four answers, then identify the chapter of this book most relevant to each answer.

Hint

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The LLM Mental Model for Engineers
blocks.src:
This is the same exercise §1.6 walks through for AI engineering itself, applied now to a concrete architectural pattern. Each of the four answers should be specific to citation verification, not generic.

**Answer:** The four answers for the citation-verification post-processor:

  1. **Pattern** : post-hoc output validation against a deterministic source-of-truth. The model produces a draft output; a deterministic verifier extracts claims (here: cited references), checks them against an authoritative source (here: a citation database or DOI lookup), and either annotates, redacts, or rejects the output before it reaches the user. This is a special case of the broader _check the model with code_ pattern, which appears in many guises (schema validation for structured output, SQL validation for query generation, tool-call argument validation). Chapter 7 (structured output) and Chapter 23 (safety in production) are where this pattern is treated systematically.

  2. **Eval** : golden set of ~100 prompts known to elicit citation-heavy outputs from the model, each manually annotated with which citations are real and which are not. The metric is _hallucination catch rate_ : of the hallucinated citations the model produces, what fraction does the post-processor flag? Plus _false-positive rate_ : how often does the post-processor flag a real citation as hallucinated because the verifier missed it? Threshold: catch rate ≥0.95, false-positive rate ≤0.05. Regression check: re-run on every prompt change, every model version change, every change to the verifier's source corpus. Chapter 4 builds the eval discipline; Chapter 5 wires it into CI.

  3. **Failure mode** : the verifier's source-of-truth is incomplete. The model cites a real but obscure paper; the verifier does not have the paper in its database; the post-processor flags it as hallucinated and removes it. The user loses a valid citation. The engineering mitigation is to design the verifier with a _graceful unknown_ response: rather than binary verified/unverified, return verified, unverified-and-not-found, or unverified-and-mismatched, and treat _unverified-and-not-found_ differently from _unverified-and-mismatched_ in the user-facing presentation. Chapter 23 covers this kind of layered failure-mode handling.

  4. **Cost** : the post-processor adds two costs. The first is the API call to the citation verifier (CrossRef is free for moderate volumes; commercial sources charge per-lookup). The second is latency: each verification adds 100–500ms depending on the verifier; if citations are frequent, this serializes on the output pipeline. The dollar cost is typically negligible; the latency cost can be significant for interactive features and may require parallel verification or a streaming-friendly architecture. Chapter 17 (multi-model routing) and Chapter 18 (cost circuit breakers) are the chapters that turn these per-call costs into a manageable budget at scale.

The exercise illustrates how the four-question rubric scales down from chapter-level concepts (§1.6 applied it to AI engineering itself) to pattern-level decisions: the same four questions tell you whether you have a real engineering plan or just a hunch.

**AI-collaboration sub-question** : How would you ask an LLM to help with this exercise, and what would you verify in its response?
