Chapters 13, 14, and 15 of this book lean on this guide repeatedly — it is the closest thing the field has to a consensus on agent design as of late 2024 — and you should read it for both the patterns and the postures. Anthropic publishes a small number of these long-form engineering guides; track the company's engineering blog for updates.

  13. **AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models** — _Chip Huyen; O'Reilly, 2025._ Huyen's second book, written explicitly for the LLM era. It overlaps with this book in scope and in some patterns — RAG, evals, agents, prompt engineering, inference economics — and is worth reading as an adjacent, sometimes complementary treatment. Where this book leans into worked-example narrative and a small number of recurring case studies (Beacon Health AI, Strata Research, Helios), Huyen leans toward broader-survey coverage and references. The two books disagree in places — most visibly on agent maturity and on how much fine-tuning to teach — and the disagreements are productive; read both and form your own view. If you finish this book and want a second pass through the same material in a different voice, this is the book to pick up next.

  14. **Eugene Yan's Writing Collection** — _Eugene Yan; eugeneyan.com, 2019–present._ Eugene Yan is what happens when a working ML engineer at Amazon decides to write deeply about everything he ships. His essays on LLM evaluation, RAG patterns, recommender systems, and applied ML systems design have become required reading inside many AI teams; the _Patterns for Building LLM-based Systems & Products_ essay alone is more practically useful than most published books. Chapter 7 of this book (embeddings and vector search) draws on Yan's writing for its examples of when classical IR beats vectors, and Chapter 24 (knowing when not to use AI) absorbs his repeated insistence that good ML engineering starts with a clear problem statement and the cheapest baseline that could possibly work. The whole site is a free engineering library; skim the table of contents, then read everything that looks relevant to what you are shipping this quarter.

blocks.en_title: Appendix A — Reading List
blocks.src:
15. **Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems** — _Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy (editors); O'Reilly, 2016._ This book has nothing to do with LLMs and everything to do with the operational discipline that AI engineering inherits. The SRE chapters on SLOs, error budgets, on-call rotations, postmortems, and graceful degradation are the substrate on which AI ops sits. Chapter 19 (observability) borrows its instrumentation vocabulary directly from the SRE book, and Chapter 21 (production eval and model upgrades) frames model upgrades as a special case of canary releases. Read the SRE book for the posture — calm, blameless, quantified, anti-heroic — that the best AI ops teams in 2026 are still trying to reach. The free HTML edition on Google's SRE site is complete and excellent; the printed book sits well on a shelf next to this one.


### Closing note

These fifteen are starting points, not endpoints. The field moves fast — Vaswani-era Transformer work is nine years old as I write this in 2026, and _Lost in the Middle_ is barely two — and the half-life of any specific recommendation is short. Track the authors and labs named here for updates: Karpathy's blog and YouTube, Lilian Weng's site, Simon Willison's daily output, Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar's continuing writing, Eugene Yan, Chip Huyen, Anthropic's and OpenAI's engineering guides, the Stanford CS329S successor courses. A 2027 second edition of this book will refresh both this reading list and the 2026 specifics that fill the rest of the chapters; what will not change is the discipline the list points at.

---

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
Two parts. The first describes ten reference architecture patterns in prose; the book ships without rendered diagrams, so the descriptions are written to be buildable from the text alone — every box, every arrow, every queue is named. The second is a catalog of agent frameworks that appear in the 2026 landscape but are deliberately not part of the Chapter 15 main-text recommendation, which keeps LangGraph, AutoGen, Pydantic AI, and Anthropic MCP.

The patterns are durable. The framework list will turn over. Read accordingly.

* * *


### Part 1 — Ten reference architecture patterns

Each pattern follows the same shape: the problem it solves, the topology in prose, when to use it, when not to use it, and which chapters of the book treat the pattern in depth.


#### Pattern 1: The Single-Provider Production Chat Surface

**What problem it solves.** One AI feature to ship — a chat surface inside an existing product, or a small standalone tool — with no need yet for multi-provider routing or a separate observability stack. The floor pattern: the first AI feature most teams ship, and what quietly powers the majority of in-production LLM features in 2026.

**Topology.** Client opens a WebSocket or SSE stream to the product's existing API gateway (Envoy, Kong, or cloud-vendor). The gateway authenticates via the existing session cookie or JWT, applies per-tenant rate limits (Redis token bucket), and forwards to a thin AI service deployed alongside other backend services. The AI service composes the prompt — system prompt from a versioned config file, user message from the request, optional history from the app database — and calls one provider's streaming endpoint (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini). Tokens stream back through the AI service to the gateway to the client. Every request is logged to the existing observability stack (Datadog, Honeycomb, or self-hosted OpenTelemetry) with three fields the team needs later: provider, model, total token count. Cost tagging happens at log-ingestion by joining against a published price table.

**When to use it.** First AI feature. Single team. Single provider acceptable for six months. Traffic under a few million requests/month. PHI/PII redaction handled by the existing data layer or not applicable. "Just call the API" is correct here.

**When NOT to use it.** Multiple AI features competing for the same budget envelope (go to Pattern 2 or 10). Regulated data in prompts without a redaction layer (Pattern 8). Eval-as-CI not in place and the surface is user-visible at scale — a future model swap will silently regress quality (Pattern 7).

**Cross-references.** Chapters 2-4 (foundational architecture), Chapter 17 (when to evolve past it), Chapter 21 (first deployment).

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
#### Pattern 2: The Multi-Model Router with Fallback

**What problem it solves.** A single provider's outage takes down the AI feature; or 60% of traffic could run on a cheaper model with no quality loss while 40% genuinely needs the frontier model. The router classifies requests and falls back on 5xx, 429, or excessive latency.

**Topology.** Before the LLM call, a router stage runs inside the AI service. Rule-based for the first version (regex on user-tier, request type, prompt-length thresholds); teams that need more graduate to a small classifier — a fine-tuned 7B or even a logistic regression on prompt features — emitting one of tier-1, tier-2, tier-3. Tier-1 routes to the frontier model (Claude Opus, GPT-5, or equivalent); tier-2 to a mid-tier model (Sonnet, GPT-4-class); tier-3 to a cheap model or a self-hosted open-weight model on the team's GPU pool. Each tier has a primary and a designated fallback provider; a circuit breaker (failure-rate threshold over a 60-second sliding window) flips traffic automatically. LiteLLM is the 2026 default that gives you provider abstraction and fallback wiring; teams with strong preferences write their own thin SDK over the raw HTTP APIs.

**When to use it.** Cost pressure is real (monthly LLM spend at salary scale, finance asking questions). Or single-provider outage would be a customer-visible incident. Or you're running A/B model experiments and want one place to encode the routing.

**When NOT to use it.** One AI feature, single-provider outage acceptable, ship-faster beats building a router. The router is a non-trivial operational surface — every model upgrade now means re-tuning thresholds.

**Cross-references.** Chapter 17 (multi-provider strategy), Chapter 18 (cost effects of routing).

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
#### Pattern 3: Production RAG with Reranker

**What problem it solves.** The LLM needs to answer questions over a corpus it wasn't trained on — customer docs, internal wikis, case law, medical literature. Vanilla vector search produces fluent answers grounded in the wrong documents; production RAG adds rewriting, hybrid retrieval, and reranking to push precision-at-k above the threshold where the LLM stops hallucinating citations.

**Topology.** Query enters a rewriting stage — a small, cheap LLM call (or a fine-tuned model) that expands into one to three search-friendly variants, handling synonyms, acronyms, and pronoun resolution against recent turns. Each variant goes through two parallel retrievers: dense embedding search against the vector store (Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector, or Turbopuffer in 2026), and BM25 lexical search against an inverted index (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or Tantivy). Candidate sets — typically 50 per retriever per variant — are deduped and merged into a pool of 100 to 200. A cross-encoder reranker (Cohere Rerank, BGE-reranker, or a fine-tuned in-house model) scores each candidate against the original query and keeps the top 8-20. Selected chunks go into the prompt with explicit document IDs. The LLM generates with structured citations referencing those IDs; a post-processing stage validates that every citation corresponds to a real chunk in the prompt and that the cited text actually appears in the source — otherwise the citation is stripped or the answer is regenerated with a stricter prompt.

**When to use it.** Corpus is too large for the context window (more than a few hundred thousand tokens). Citations are required for trust, regulatory, or product reasons. Vanilla vector search has produced enough hallucinated-citation incidents to justify reranking infrastructure.

**When NOT to use it.** Corpus is small enough to stuff in context (under 200k tokens) — long-context models in 2026 often outperform half-built RAG. Or queries don't need grounding (creative writing, brainstorming, code generation against training data).

**Cross-references.** Chapter 9 (vector retrieval), Chapter 10 (reranking and hybrid), Chapter 11 (citations and post-processing).

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
#### Pattern 4: Vision-First Document Ingestion

**What problem it solves.** PDFs are not text. Text-extraction libraries (pdfminer, PyMuPDF) produce a stream of characters with no layout, no tables, no figures, and no awareness that a two-column journal article should be read column-by-column. The result is RAG over garbage. Vision-first ingestion treats each page as an image and uses a VLM to extract structured content directly.

**Topology.** PDF lands in object storage (S3, GCS) with a job tag. A worker pulls the job, splits the PDF into PNG or JPEG renders at 200 DPI (PyMuPDF or pdf2image), and emits one image per page to a queue. A pool of VLM workers (Claude vision, GPT-4-class vision, Gemini Pro Vision, or self-hosted Qwen-VL) consumes the queue. Per page, the worker calls the VLM with a structured-extraction prompt: narrative text in reading order, tables as JSON, figures with captions, section headings with hierarchy level, and page metadata (page number, document ID, layout class). Output is one JSON document per page, validated against a Pydantic schema. A normalization stage joins pages into a single document tree (section continuity, table-spans-pages, footnote resolution). The normalized document is chunked semantically (on section boundaries, never split a table, attach figure captions to their figures), and chunks are indexed for retrieval as in Pattern 3 — with richer metadata (section path, page number, table-or-prose flag) the reranker and prompt-construction stages can exploit.

**When to use it.** Source corpus is PDFs with non-trivial layout — academic papers, regulatory filings, medical records, contracts, financial statements with tables. Strata Research's legal-tech platform is canonical: case law is unusable through naive text extraction but a VLM pipeline yields clean, citable structure.

**When NOT to use it.** Documents are already in HTML, Markdown, or other structured formats. Or simple enough that pdfminer-plus-cleanup gets 95% of the way. VLM ingestion is 10-50x more expensive per page than text extraction; volume matters.

**Cross-references.** Chapter 12 (multimodal ingestion).

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
#### Pattern 5: Bounded Agent with Tool Catalog

**What problem it solves.** A single LLM call can't do the work — the task requires reading a database, calling an API, writing a file, and iterating on intermediate results. A naive agent loop ("LLM, here are tools, go") runs away: infinite iteration, exploding cost, repeated identical tool calls when the model gets stuck. The bounded agent is the production-safe variant.

**Topology.** User goal enters an agent service that maintains per-session state: iteration count, cumulative token cost, tool-call history (arguments hashed for dedup), budget envelope. The loop is explicit: (1) compose the prompt — system instruction, goal, running scratchpad, tool catalog; (2) call the LLM; (3) if the LLM emits a tool call, dedup against history (identical name plus arguments within the last N iterations is rejected and the model is told it already tried that), then execute in a sandbox — gVisor, Firecracker, or a process-isolated subprocess with a strict syscall allowlist — with a per-call timeout (5-30 s) and result-size cap (4-16 KB); (4) append the result to the scratchpad; (5) check circuit breakers — iteration cap (10-30), cost cap (cumulative tokens × unit price), wall-clock cap (60-300 s) — and abort gracefully if any trips. Full trajectory (every prompt, response, tool call, result) is logged with a single trajectory ID so post-mortems are tractable.

**When to use it.** The task genuinely requires tool use and iteration. Tools have meaningful side effects (writes, payments, irreversible operations) that demand a sandbox. You've already shipped one or two non-agent AI features and have an observability story.

**When NOT to use it.** The task can be solved with one LLM call plus structured output. Or the team has never shipped a production AI feature and is reaching for an agent because of hype — most 2025 "agent" use cases turned out to be one-call-plus-RAG in disguise.

**Cross-references.** Chapter 13 (the agent loop), Chapter 14 (tool catalogs and sandboxing).

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
#### Pattern 6: Orchestrator-and-Workers Multi-Agent

**What problem it solves.** A single agent's context window can't hold all the state for a complex task: research the company, draft three email variants, generate matching social-media copy, compose a follow-up plan. Each sub-task wants a different prompt, tool catalog, and possibly a different model. The pattern decomposes across specialized workers and aggregates.

**Topology.** Goal enters an orchestrator agent — typically a frontier model with a system prompt that specializes it for planning and routing rather than execution. The orchestrator emits a structured plan: sub-tasks tagged with worker type ("research-worker", "writing-worker", "code-worker") and inputs. The plan goes onto a work queue (Celery, Temporal, or a custom queue over Postgres/Redis). Worker pools — one per type, each running its own agent loop with its own tools and often its own model — consume sub-tasks and emit results. The orchestrator polls (or subscribes via Temporal); when all sub-tasks complete, it composes the final response. Cross-cutting concerns — overall iteration cap, budget envelope, cross-worker dedup — live with the orchestrator. Helios, the multi-agent legal-research extension to Strata's platform, is this pattern: decompose a question into "find precedents", "summarize statutes", "draft argument", "check citations", with specialized workers for each.

**When to use it.** Task decomposes naturally along worker specializations, sub-tasks parallelize for latency wins, you've already shipped Pattern 5. Team is large enough that different specialists own different worker types.

**When NOT to use it.** Sub-tasks have heavy interdependencies that defeat parallelism. Small team; the operational overhead of multiple worker pools isn't justified. You're seduced by an architecture diagram — in 2026 most production "multi-agent" systems would be simpler and more reliable as a single Pattern 5 agent with a richer tool catalog.

**Cross-references.** Chapter 15 (multi-agent architectures and the 2026 framework landscape).

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
#### Pattern 7: Eval-as-CI Gate

**What problem it solves.** A prompt change, a model upgrade, or a RAG refactor silently regresses quality. The regression is discovered weeks later through customer complaints; the offending change is buried under twenty unrelated commits and rolling back is expensive. Eval-as-CI moves quality checks to the moment of change.

**Topology.** The team maintains a golden eval set — 100 to 1,000 input/expected-output pairs, versioned in git alongside code, with a documented refresh cadence (typically quarterly, with a "what changed and why" note in the eval commit). A PR touching prompt files, model identifiers, or any code on the LLM-call path triggers a CI job. The job runs the candidate against the golden set, computes metrics (exact-match for structured tasks; LLM-as-judge for open-ended tasks, with the judge calibrated against human-labeled subsets), and posts the results as a PR comment with a diff against the merge-base baseline. If any metric regresses beyond a published threshold — typically 2-5 percentage points on the primary metric, or any drop on a pinned must-not-regress subset — CI fails and the PR is blocked. Thresholds and the pinned subset are themselves versioned; loosening a threshold requires its own PR with justification. Costs are bounded by running a cheap reproducible subset on every push and the full set only on merge-base updates or explicit `/run-full-eval` comments.

**When to use it.** You've regretted at least one silent regression that reached customers. CI infrastructure is in place (GitHub Actions, Buildkite, Jenkins). The eval set is curatable — the team can articulate "good" with enough specificity to write 100 examples.

**When NOT to use it.** You haven't yet figured out what good looks like — eval-as-CI before calibration will block PRs on noise. Or the product is so early that prompts change daily and there's no stable target. Invest in evals first (Chapter 5); flip the CI gate on when the set is stable.

**Cross-references.** Chapter 4 (eval design and LLM-as-judge calibration), Chapter 5 (evals from scratch and binding workflow #1, the GitHub Actions eval-as-CI gate), Chapter 21 (production-eval drift detection and model-upgrade workflow), Chapter 24 (eval-as-CI in the development workflow).

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
#### Pattern 8: Observability with PHI Redaction (Regulated)

**What problem it solves.** HIPAA covered entity, GDPR sensitive-category processor, PCI handler. The standard observability story — ship every prompt and response to Datadog or Honeycomb — is a compliance violation: prompts carry PHI/PII the vendor isn't a Business Associate for. You still need traces. Beacon Health AI lives in this constraint and built the pattern.

**Topology.** Every LLM call emits an OpenTelemetry trace from the AI service. Before the trace leaves the network boundary, it passes through a redaction sidecar — a small Go or Rust service (low latency matters; redaction is on the ingestion critical path) that scans prompt and response spans. The detector is layered: regex for structured identifiers (SSN, MRN, account numbers, email, phone); NER (spaCy with a HIPAA-Safe-Harbor entity set, or a fine-tuned BERT-class model) for free-text PHI (names, addresses, dates); and a final LLM pass for adversarial cases, run only when prior layers agree the text is "probably clean" so you don't pay the LLM tax on the majority of traces. Detected entities are replaced with typed tokens (`[NAME_1]`, `[DOB_1]`) preserving co-reference. The redacted trace ships to the trace store — self-hosted Langfuse for LLM-observability features, self-hosted Tempo or Jaeger for spans only. Grafana dashboards show latency, cost, error rate, and a per-tenant quality proxy. The original un-redacted trace lives in a separate raw-trace vault inside the BAA-covered data plane with short retention (24-72 hours) and access-audited reads — for incident response only, never routine dashboards.

**When to use it.** HIPAA, PCI, GDPR special category, or any regime where prompt contents are themselves regulated. The redaction layer pays for itself the first time legal asks "what does our observability vendor see?"

**When NOT to use it.** Data is not regulated. Redaction adds 20-100 ms to every trace ingest and a meaningful operational surface to monitor; don't take it on without the compliance justification.

**Cross-references.** Chapter 19 (observability for LLM systems, including §19.7's PHI-redaction patterns and §19.6's HIPAA tension); Chapter 23 (output-safety and the four-layer prompt-injection defense, which reuses the same PII patterns).

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
#### Pattern 9: Voice Agent with Fallback to Text

**What problem it solves.** Product is voice-first — clinical scribe, customer-support agent, hands-free assistant — but voice is unreliable: STT mis-hears, TTS sounds wrong on rare phonemes, EOT detection cuts the user off, a dropped packet derails a turn. The pattern is the production-grade voice loop with graceful text fallback.

**Topology.** Client opens a bidirectional audio stream (WebRTC, or a vendor SDK like LiveKit or Daily) to a voice-agent service. STT runs in streaming mode (Deepgram, Whisper-streaming, ElevenLabs Scribe) emitting partial transcripts every 200-500 ms. An EOT detector — a small classifier over partials (VAD, pause length, prosodic cues) or a dedicated EOT model — decides when the user is done. On EOT, the finalized transcript flows to the LLM (Pattern 1 or 5 depending on tool use). The LLM response streams token-by-token into a streaming TTS (ElevenLabs, Cartesia, or a vendor's native streaming TTS); audio frames stream to the client. An interruption handler runs in parallel: if the client detects user speech while TTS is playing, the service cancels in-flight TTS, flushes the LLM stream, and starts a new turn. If any stage fails — STT confidence below threshold, TTS error, audio channel stall — a fallback opens a text panel; the user sees the transcript and can type, with the LLM continuing in text-only mode. Voice attempts reconnect in the background; on success the client offers "resume voice".

**When to use it.** Voice is a first-class product surface. Team has audio-engineering capability (or vendor partnership) and is prepared to debug RTC issues. Latency budget is tight (sub-700 ms turn latency for natural conversation, sub-300 ms ideal) and you've measured it.

**When NOT to use it.** Voice is "nice to have" or a demo. Voice agents are an order of magnitude more operational work than text agents; don't take the work unless voice is the product.

**Cross-references.** Chapter 20 (voice and multimodal interfaces in production).

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
#### Pattern 10: Cost-Optimized Multi-Tier Cache Stack

**What problem it solves.** The LLM bill is the largest engineering line item. Per-token costs have fallen year over year but volume has grown faster. The cache stack squeezes the bill by serving repeated and similar requests without hitting the model, and by moving non-urgent work to cheaper async lanes.

**Topology.** Layers run in front of the LLM call, each cheaper and faster than the next. Layer 1, exact-match application cache: Redis or Memcached lookup keyed by a hash of `(normalized prompt, model, temperature, tools, system prompt version)`; TTL of minutes to hours; hit rate 5-20% on user surfaces, higher on automated workloads. Layer 2, semantic cache: compute the prompt's embedding (reuse the RAG embedder), vector-lookup in a small dedicated index for prior prompts above cosine threshold (0.95-0.98); return cached response if threshold and freshness check pass. Mis-thresholded semantic caches return wrong answers — 0.92 will cheerfully misroute — so calibrate against an eval set and dashboard hit rate. Layer 3, provider prompt caching: Anthropic's feature (and similar at OpenAI and Gemini in 2026) discounts repeated prefix tokens; structure the prompt with long stable parts (system prompt, tool catalog, session-stable RAG context) at the front. Layer 4, batch endpoint: for non-synchronous workloads (overnight analytics, doc-processing, eval runs), submit to the provider's batch API at ~50% discount with a 24-hour SLA. Only after all four miss does the request hit the synchronous endpoint. Each layer is observable: hit rate, hit-rate-by-tenant, "cost saved this month" on the dashboard.

**When to use it.** LLM spend at six figures annually or higher. Engineering bandwidth to operate caches (they will go stale, they will return wrong answers, you need a runbook). Traffic pattern has structural repetition (same user asks similar questions, system-prompt-plus-context mostly stable across requests).

**When NOT to use it.** Traffic is mostly unique and caches won't hit. Or you haven't measured a hit-rate ceiling and are over-engineering pre-emptively. Start with Layer 1 and Layer 3; add 2 and 4 when data says they pay off.

**Cross-references.** Chapter 18 (cost optimization), Chapter 17 (provider strategy and prompt caching).

* * *

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
### Part 2 — Agent framework catalog (beyond Ch 15's four named)

Chapter 15 picks four for the main text: LangGraph (LangChain-ecosystem default), AutoGen (Microsoft Research's multi-agent conversation framework), Pydantic AI (lightweight, type-safe), and Anthropic MCP (tool-integration protocol). The recommendation is opinionated: Pydantic AI or hand-rolled for new agents at small teams; LangGraph for LangChain shops; MCP wherever portable tool integration matters.

The broader 2026 landscape includes the following entrants. Table is brief; the paragraphs below carry the substance.

Framework | Position | Consider when | Skip when  
---|---|---|---  
CrewAI | Multi-agent crews with role-based abstractions | The mental model of "role-playing agents" matches your design instinct and you're prototyping fast | You need production-grade observability, custom routing, or fine control of the agent loop  
OpenAI Swarm (experimental) | Lightweight multi-agent reference implementation | You're inside the OpenAI ecosystem and want a minimal multi-agent demo on top of the Responses API | You need a maintained, supported framework — Swarm is an explicit research artifact  
Haystack 2 | RAG-first orchestration with agent extensions | RAG is the dominant workload and you want a pipeline framework rather than an agent framework | The center of gravity is agent-loop work; Haystack's pipelines fit RAG better than open-ended agents  
LlamaIndex | RAG framework with lightweight agent loops | You're already using LlamaIndex for retrieval and want to extend, not replace | You haven't already committed to LlamaIndex — there's no strong agent-side reason to start here in 2026  
DSPy | Prompt and program optimization (not strictly an agent framework) | You need a principled way to optimize prompts and few-shot exemplars against an objective metric | You want a runtime agent framework — DSPy is a compiler-style tool, not a runtime  
Smolagents | Hugging Face's minimal code-based agent framework | You want code-as-the-action-space (the agent writes Python rather than calling structured tools) and you trust the sandbox story | You need structured tool calling, broad provider support, or a polished production story  
  
**CrewAI.** Central abstraction is the "crew" — role-defined agents ("researcher", "writer", "editor") working together. The strength is conceptual: the role model maps cleanly to how product teams describe what they want, which makes prototyping fast and accessible to PMs and designers authoring crews. The weakness is the gap to production: observability, custom-routing hooks, and fine control over the per-turn loop are thinner than LangGraph's or Pydantic AI's in 2026. Teams that adopt CrewAI for a POC and then ship frequently re-implement on a more configurable framework. Consider for early exploration; expect a migration if you scale.

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
**OpenAI Swarm.** Released in 2024 as an educational reference for lightweight multi-agent patterns over OpenAI's Responses API. The core abstraction is the "handoff" — an agent hands the conversation to another by returning the next agent as its output. Swarm is intentionally minimal, intentionally unmaintained, and intentionally not a production framework; OpenAI's stated stance is "use this to learn the pattern, then build your own". The handoff pattern shows up inside LangGraph and AutoGen as a sub-case. Consider for understanding the pattern or single-developer experiments inside the OpenAI ecosystem. Skip for anything you intend to maintain past the prototype.

**Haystack 2.** The 2024 rewrite of the original Haystack RAG framework, with first-class pipeline abstractions and agent extensions added in 2025. Center of gravity is retrieval and document processing; pipelines compose retrievers, rankers, prompt builders, and generators into directed graphs that resemble Pattern 3 above. Agent extensions wrap the pipeline as a tool the LLM can invoke. Mature, well-documented, with a clear deployment story (Haystack-as-a-Service, or self-hosted under FastAPI). Consider when RAG is the dominant workload and the team prefers a pipeline mental model over a graph or typed-function one. Skip when agent work is the main thing and RAG is a sub-component; LangGraph or Pydantic AI fit better there and you compose retrieval yourself.

**LlamaIndex.** Originally GPT Index in 2022, LlamaIndex is the long-standing RAG framework that gradually grew an agent layer (originally ReAct-style, then a more general runtime, then "workflows" in 2024-25 that resemble LangGraph graphs). Retrieval side is excellent — broad connectors, mature query engines, strong out-of-the-box performance. Agent side is competent but lacks a clear differentiator over LangGraph or Pydantic AI in 2026. If you're already on LlamaIndex for retrieval, extend with its agent layer rather than add a second framework. Greenfield, the agent side alone is not a reason to start here; pick your agent framework first and your retrieval stack separately.

**DSPy.** Not strictly an agent framework — a programming model where the developer writes "modules" with declared input/output signatures, and DSPy compiles them by optimizing prompts and few-shot exemplars against a developer-provided metric. The relationship to the four main-text frameworks is orthogonal: DSPy can produce the prompts that LangGraph nodes or Pydantic AI agents use. Strength is principled optimization — given a clear metric and meaningful training examples, DSPy finds prompt configurations hand-writing struggles to match. Weakness is that compilation is a separate phase; you compile, ship the artifact, and run on a different framework. Consider when you have a measurable objective, an eval set you trust, and bandwidth for an additional build phase. Skip when you need a runtime framework — DSPy is the wrong layer.

blocks.en_title: Appendix B — Reference Architecture Catalog
blocks.src:
**Smolagents.** Hugging Face, late 2024/early 2025; deliberately small (the name is the thesis). Distinctive design choice: the action space is Python code rather than structured tool calls. The agent generates a snippet that calls available tools as functions, the snippet runs in a sandbox, the result feeds back. Expressivity is high (compose tools, loop, branch, use intermediate variables in one step) and the codebase is small enough to read end-to-end. Risks are real: code-as-action depends on a trustworthy sandbox with a richer attack surface (Turing-complete by design), and provider support is thinner than the main-text four. Consider when code-as-action fits the problem (data-analysis, computational tasks) and the team can harden a sandbox. Skip when structured tool calling is sufficient.

* * *


### Closing note

The architecture patterns above are durable. The seven most teams use — single-provider chat, multi-model router, production RAG with reranker, vision-first ingestion, bounded agent, eval-as-CI, multi-tier caching — are versions of patterns that worked in 2024, work in 2026, and will work in 2028 even if providers, models, and frameworks have all changed. The other three (multi-agent orchestrator, regulated observability, voice with fallback) are sub-specialties that come up in particular settings and outlast the specific tools they're built with.

The framework landscape is the opposite. Of the ten frameworks named between Ch 15 and this appendix, a safe 2028 prediction is that at least three will be deprecated, at least two absorbed into larger ecosystems, and at least one framework not yet announced in 2026 will be the new conventional wisdom. The implication: pick frameworks for organizational fit — the team's language, the existing dependency graph, tolerance for framework opinion versus DIY control, availability of support contracts if procurement cares — and never for hype. The architecture survives the framework. Teams that internalize this ship more and panic less when the landscape moves under them.

---

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
A working glossary of ~280 AI engineering terms an engineer building production LLM systems in 2026 should know. Definitions are operational (how the term is used in practice), not encyclopedic. Cross-references to chapters where the term is developed are given as (Ch N).


### A

**A/B testing** : Running two model or prompt variants against live traffic with a split rule, then comparing outcomes on predefined metrics before promoting a winner (Ch 21, §21.4).

**Advanced RAG** : A RAG pipeline that adds query rewriting, hybrid retrieval, reranking, and citation grounding on top of naive retrieve-then-generate. The baseline expectation for production systems in 2026 (Ch 10).

**Agent** : An LLM-driven loop that selects tools, observes results, and decides the next step toward a goal. Always bounded by iteration and cost caps in production (Ch 14, §14.1).

**AI code review** : Using LLMs to review diffs for defects, style, or policy violations as a CI step. Treated as one signal among many, not as a gate (Ch 24, §24.3).

**AI engineer** : Engineer who builds production systems on top of foundation models: prompts, RAG, agents, evals, infrastructure. Distinct from ML engineer (who trains models) and AI product engineer (who owns features) (Ch 24, §24.1).

**AI Gateway** : Reverse-proxy layer in front of model providers that handles routing, key management, rate limits, caching, and observability. Examples: Cloudflare AI Gateway, Kong AI Gateway, Portkey (Ch 17).

**AI ops** : Operational role focused on monitoring, incident response, cost control, and capacity for AI systems in production (Ch 24, §24.1).

**AI product engineer** : Engineer who owns end-to-end AI features including UX, eval design, and growth metrics, in addition to the underlying pipeline (Ch 24, §24.1).

**Anyscale** : Managed Ray platform used for distributed training, batch inference, and fine-tuning of open-weight models (Ch 22, §22.4).

**Anthropic** : Provider of the Claude model family. Operationally relevant for `cache_control`, dated snapshot conventions, and the MCP specification (Ch 3, Ch 14).

**Apple Intelligence** : Apple's on-device + cloud AI system that runs small models locally and routes larger requests to Private Cloud Compute. A reference pattern for hybrid edge inference (Ch 22, §22.6).

**Arize** : Observability platform for AI systems with strong focus on drift detection and embedding monitoring (Ch 19, §19.3).

**Assistant message** : A message turn produced by the model in a multi-turn conversation. Distinct from system, user, and tool messages (Ch 3, §3.1).

**Attention** : The mechanism by which a transformer weighs prior tokens when predicting the next one. Operationally relevant because attention cost scales with context length (Ch 2, §2.4).

**AutoGen** : Microsoft's multi-agent framework built around conversational agents that exchange messages. One of several orchestration choices alongside LangGraph and Pydantic AI (Ch 15, §15.4).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### B

**BAA** : Business Associate Agreement. A HIPAA-required contract between a covered entity and any vendor that processes PHI on its behalf. No BAA, no PHI through that vendor (Ch 19, §19.6).

**Base model** : A pretrained model before any instruction tuning or RLHF. Useful for completion-style tasks; rarely used directly for chat (Ch 2, §2.3).

**Batch inference** : Submitting requests asynchronously for processing within a deadline (usually 24h) at ~50% discount. Use for evals, backfills, and any non-interactive workload (Ch 18, §18.5).

**Beam search** : Decoding strategy that keeps the top-k partial sequences. Largely replaced by sampling for LLMs because it produces bland, repetitive text (Ch 2, §2.5).

**BM25** : Classical lexical retrieval scoring based on term frequency and document length. Still essential as the keyword half of hybrid search (Ch 10, §10.5).

**Bounded agent** : An agent constrained by explicit caps on iterations, tool calls, tokens, wall time, and dollars. The only kind of agent that ships to production (Ch 14, §14.4).

**BPE** : Byte-Pair Encoding. The dominant tokenization algorithm: starts from bytes and greedily merges the most frequent adjacent pairs until the target vocabulary size is reached (Ch 2, §2.2).

**Build-vs-buy** : The decision matrix for whether to construct a layer of the AI stack in-house or adopt a vendor. The default answer in 2026 is buy for everything except the parts that are your differentiator (Ch 16, §16.3).

**Bi-encoder** : Architecture that encodes query and document independently, enabling pre-computed document embeddings and fast nearest-neighbor search. The first-stage retriever in most RAG systems (Ch 10, §10.5).

**Backfill** : Re-running an updated pipeline over historical inputs to refresh outputs. A common use case for batch inference (Ch 18, §18.5).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### C

**Cache hit rate** : Fraction of prompt tokens served from a provider's prompt cache. The single most leveraged cost-and-latency metric for high-volume LLM systems (Ch 18, §18.2).

**cache_control** : Anthropic API field that marks a content block as a cache breakpoint. Up to four breakpoints per request; everything before each is cached (Ch 18, §18.2).

**Calibration** : How well a model's stated confidence matches its actual accuracy. A calibrated model that says "70% sure" is right 70% of the time (Ch 5, §5.4).

**Canary deployment** : Routing a small fraction of traffic to a new model or prompt version, monitoring metrics, and rolling forward or back based on results (Ch 21, §21.6).

**Can-we-eval gate** : Pre-build check that a proposed feature has measurable success criteria. If you can't write the eval, you can't build the feature (Ch 24, §24.4).

**Capability matrix** : A team's mapping of approaches (rules / classical ML / LLM with prompt / RAG / agent / hybrid / don't use AI) to a task, used to make the build-or-not decision deliberately rather than by hype-chasing (Ch 24, §24.7).

**Cartesia** : Low-latency TTS provider known for natural prosody and sub-100ms time-to-first-audio (Ch 20, §20.4).

**Chroma** : Open-source vector database focused on developer ergonomics. Good for prototypes and small-to-medium corpora (Ch 10, §10.4).

**Chunking** : Splitting source documents into retrieval units. Quality of chunking sets the ceiling on RAG quality (Ch 9, §9.3).

**Citation grounding** : Requiring the model to attach source spans to claims and verifying that the cited spans support them. The defense against fluent hallucination in RAG (Ch 11, §11.7).

**Cloudflare AI Gateway** : Edge-deployed gateway with built-in caching, rate limiting, and analytics across all major providers. Strong default for global low-latency routing (Ch 17, §17.3).

**CoT** : Chain-of-thought. Prompting the model to reason in intermediate steps before answering. Largely subsumed by built-in reasoning modes in 2026, but still relevant for non-reasoning models (Ch 6, §6.2).

**ColPali** : Late-interaction multimodal retriever that embeds document pages as patches without OCR. The state-of-the-art for visual document RAG in 2026 (Ch 12, §12.3).

**Computer use** : Capability where the model controls a virtual desktop via screenshots and mouse/keyboard actions. Powerful, slow, and security-critical (Ch 15, §15.6).

**Confidence calibration** : See _calibration_. In safety contexts, the property that lets a system refuse or escalate when uncertain rather than confabulate (Ch 23, §23.5).

**Constrained decoding** : Restricting the model's next-token distribution to match a grammar or schema. The reliable path to valid JSON; supported natively by most providers in 2026 (Ch 7, §7.5).

**Content filtering** : Pre- or post-generation classifiers that block outputs containing prohibited content (violence, sexual content involving minors, self-harm, etc.) (Ch 23, §23.2).

**Context budget** : The token allocation for each section of a prompt (system, retrieval, history, query). Set explicitly, not implicitly (Ch 8, §8.2).

**Context engineering** : The discipline of selecting, compressing, and ordering what goes into the context window. Replaced "prompt engineering" as the central skill in 2026 (Ch 8, §8.1).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
**Context window** : The maximum number of tokens a model can attend to in one call. Quoted limits are best-case; effective limits are smaller due to lost-in-the-middle effects (Ch 2, §2.4).

**Correlated-family bias** : When an LLM judge favors outputs from models in its own family (same vendor or training lineage). Mitigated by judge rotation (Ch 5, §5.6).

**Cost circuit breaker** : Hard cap on per-request or per-session spend that aborts execution when crossed. Mandatory for agents (Ch 14, §14.4).

**Cross-encoder** : A model that jointly encodes a query and a candidate document to produce a relevance score. More accurate than bi-encoders but too slow for first-pass retrieval; used as reranker (Ch 11, §11.1).

**Cost per task** : The fully loaded LLM spend to complete one user-visible unit of work (one answer, one ticket, one document). The right cost metric for product decisions (Ch 18, §18.1).

**Chain-of-thought** : See _CoT_ (Ch 6, §6.2).

**Claude** : Anthropic's model family. The reference platform for prompt caching, MCP, and long-context use cases in this book (Ch 3).

**Continuous batching** : Inference-server technique that interleaves requests at the token level, dramatically improving GPU utilization. The reason vLLM and TGI outperform naive serving (Ch 22, §22.5).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### D

**Dated version** : Pinning a model identifier to a specific date snapshot (e.g., `claude-opus-4-7-20260315`) rather than a floating alias. Required for reproducible behavior (Ch 3, §3.1).

**Debate** : Multi-agent pattern where two or more agents argue opposing positions and a judge picks the winner. Useful for hard analytic tasks; rarely worth the cost otherwise (Ch 15, §15.3).

**Deepgram** : STT provider known for low latency and strong real-time streaming. Common voice-stack choice (Ch 20, §20.3).

**DeepSeek** : Chinese open-weight model family with strong reasoning performance at low cost. Notable for V3 and R1 releases (Ch 22, §22.1).

**Deprecation** : A provider's planned retirement of a model snapshot. In 2026, typical notice is 6-12 months with a forced cutover thereafter (Ch 3, §3.11).

**Dimension** : The vector length of an embedding (e.g., 1024, 1536, 3072). Higher dimensions cost more storage and compute; Matryoshka embeddings let you truncate at retrieval time (Ch 10, §10.3).

**Discriminated union** : A Pydantic/TypeScript pattern where a tag field selects which schema variant applies. The clean way to model "one of N response shapes" in structured output (Ch 7, §7.4).

**Distillation** : Training a smaller model to match a larger one's outputs. The practical path to 5-10x cost reduction once you have a stable workload (Ch 18, §18.6).

**DPO** : Direct Preference Optimization. Fine-tuning method that trains directly on (chosen, rejected) pairs without a separate reward model. Lighter alternative to RLHF (Ch 2, §2.3).

**Drift detection** : Monitoring statistical changes in inputs, outputs, or embedding distributions over time. Early-warning signal for silent regressions (Ch 21, §21.2 and §21.7).

**DSPy** : Framework for programmatically composing and optimizing LLM pipelines. Pairs with MIPRO for automatic prompt tuning (Ch 6, §6.3).

**Dead-letter queue** : A holding area for requests that failed permanently after exhausting retries. Required for batch pipelines so failures don't block progress (Ch 18, §18.5).

**Data residency** : Regulatory or contractual requirement that data stay in specific geographies. Constrains gateway routing and storage choices (Ch 19, §19.6).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### E

**E2B** : Sandboxing service offering ephemeral Linux containers for agent code execution. Common choice for "run this LLM-written code" workloads (Ch 13, §13.5).

**Edge inference** : Running models on devices near the user (phones, laptops, edge servers) rather than in centralized clouds. Trades capacity for latency and privacy (Ch 22, §22.6).

**ElevenLabs Conversational AI** : Voice agent platform combining ElevenLabs TTS with STT and turn-taking logic. Strong on voice quality (Ch 20, §20.5).

**Embedding** : A dense vector representation of text (or other modality) where semantic similarity corresponds to vector distance. Foundation of retrieval (Ch 10, §10.1).

**Embedding model** : The model that produces embeddings. Choice matters: domain, dimension, max sequence length, and license all factor in (Ch 10, §10.2).

**End-of-turn detection** : Deciding when the user has finished speaking. The hardest unsolved problem in voice agents in 2026 (Ch 20, §20.6).

**End-to-end voice model** : A model that processes audio in and produces audio out without a separate STT/LLM/TTS pipeline. Lower latency, less control over individual stages (Ch 20, §20.7).

**EOT** : End-of-turn. See _end-of-turn detection_ (Ch 20, §20.6).

**Ephemeral cache** : Provider prompt cache that lives for a few minutes (typically 5) after the last hit. The cost trade-off: cheap to write, costs zero once expired (Ch 18, §18.2).

**Episodic memory** : Agent memory of specific past interactions, retrieved by similarity to the current situation. Distinct from long-term semantic memory (Ch 14, §14.5).

**Eval-as-CI** : Running evaluations on every PR and blocking merges that regress key metrics. The discipline that separates serious teams from prototypers (Ch 5, §5.7).

**Eval-driven development** : Defining the eval before writing the prompt or pipeline. Inverts the usual flow and forces clarity on success (Ch 4 §4.1; Ch 24 §24.2 phase 2).

**Eval store** : Persistent system that holds eval definitions, runs, and results. Lets you compare any two versions historically without rerunning (Ch 5, §5.8).

**Exponential backoff** : Retry strategy that doubles the wait between attempts (with jitter). The default for transient API failures (Ch 3, §3.5).

**Evaluation harness** : The code that runs eval items through the system under test, collects outputs, and applies graders. Distinct from the eval _definitions_ it executes (Ch 5, §5.7).

**Eval slice** : A named subset of the eval set (e.g., "Spanish queries", "long-context", "PII-bearing"). Slicing reveals regressions that aggregate scores hide (Ch 5, §5.8).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### F

**Fallback chain** : An ordered list of models or providers attempted in sequence on failure. Combined with circuit breakers, the standard reliability pattern (Ch 17, §17.5).

**Feasibility spike** : A 1-3 day timeboxed prototype to test whether an AI feature is achievable. Almost always cheaper than arguing about it (Ch 24, §24.6).

**Fine-tuning** : Continuing training on task-specific data. In 2026, usually means LoRA/QLoRA on open weights or hosted fine-tuning of a base model (Ch 2, §2.3, Ch 22, §22.3).

**Fine-tune half-life** : The time before a fine-tuned model is outclassed by a newer base model in zero-shot mode. Currently 6-12 months for most tasks (Ch 22, §22.3).

**Firecracker** : AWS micro-VM technology used by Lambda and some sandboxing services. Much stronger isolation than containers at slightly higher startup cost (Ch 13, §13.5).

**Function calling** : Provider-specific name for tool use, where the model returns a structured call to a named function. Mechanically equivalent to tool use (Ch 13, §13.1).

**Few-shot** : Including a small number of input-output examples in the prompt to demonstrate the task. Often outperformed by fine-tuning at high volume, but cheaper to iterate (Ch 6, §6.2).


### G

**Gemini Live** : Google's real-time multimodal API supporting voice and video input with low-latency output. Direct competitor to OpenAI Realtime (Ch 20, §20.5).

**Gemma** : Google's open-weight model family. Useful for on-device and small-server deployments (Ch 22, §22.1).

**Golden set** : A small (50-500 example) hand-curated dataset with reference answers. The bedrock of an eval suite; everything else builds on it (Ch 4, §4.3).

**Graceful degradation** : Designing the system so partial failures (model unavailable, retrieval empty, tool errored) produce a useful response rather than a stack trace (Ch 23, §23.6).

**gVisor** : Google's user-space kernel that intercepts syscalls, providing container-level isolation with VM-level safety. Common sandbox choice (Ch 13, §13.5).

**GPU hours** : The standard unit of training and self-hosted inference cost. Reasoning in GPU-hours rather than dollars makes provider-vs-self comparisons honest (Ch 22, §22.5).

**Guardrail** : A pre- or post-generation check that enforces a policy (length, format, content, cost). The umbrella term for output safety + token-budget controls (Ch 23, §23.1).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### H

**Hallucination** : Confident, fluent output that is factually wrong. Mitigated but not eliminated by RAG, citation grounding, and refusal training (Ch 2, §2.6, Ch 11, §11.7).

**Helicone** : Open-source LLM observability platform with strong cost and cache analytics. Lightweight alternative to Langfuse (Ch 19, §19.3).

**Hierarchical context** : Organizing prompt context as a tree (system → task → retrieval → query) rather than a flat list. Improves model adherence to instructions (Ch 8, §8.4).

**Hierarchical decomposition** : Multi-agent pattern where a top-level agent breaks a goal into subgoals dispatched to specialized agents. The "orchestrator-workers" pattern (Ch 15, §15.2).

**HIPAA** : U.S. healthcare privacy regulation governing PHI. Defines what counts as PHI, who can access it, and the BAA framework for vendors (Ch 19, §19.6).

**Hybrid search** : Combining lexical (BM25) and semantic (vector) retrieval, usually fused with RRF. The default retrieval setup in 2026 (Ch 10, §10.5).

**HyDE** : Hypothetical Document Embeddings. Query expansion technique that generates a fake "ideal answer" and embeds it instead of the original query. Useful when queries are much shorter than documents (Ch 11, §11.2).

**Human-in-the-loop** : Workflow where humans approve, edit, or override LLM outputs before they take effect. The right default for any irreversible action (Ch 13, §13.6).


### I

**"I don't know" pattern** : Explicit training or prompting to make the model refuse or defer when evidence is insufficient. Calibration's behavioral expression (Ch 23, §23.5).

**Idempotency** : A request that produces the same effect whether sent once or many times. Provider idempotency keys let you safely retry without double-charging or double-acting (Ch 3, §3.5).

**Indirect prompt injection** : Attack where malicious instructions are embedded in retrieved or tool-fetched content (web pages, documents, emails). The hardest class of LLM security threat (Ch 23, §23.3).

**Instruct model** : A base model that has been instruction-tuned and aligned. What you almost always actually want to call (Ch 2, §2.3).

**Interruption handling** : Logic that detects when the user starts speaking over the agent and stops or yields. Essential for natural voice UX (Ch 20, §20.6).

**In-trajectory summarization** : Compressing prior steps of an agent's trajectory into a summary when the context window gets tight. The standard memory-pressure relief (Ch 14, §14.5).

**Iteration cap** : The maximum number of think-act-observe cycles an agent may run before forced termination. Always set; default values are too high (Ch 14, §14.4).

**Inference cost** : The variable cost of running a model in production, dominated by tokens for hosted models and GPU time for self-hosted (Ch 18, §18.1).

**Inference endpoint** : A URL exposing a model for inference, whether hosted by a provider or self-deployed (Ch 22, §22.5).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### J

**Jailbreak** : A prompt or input designed to make the model bypass its safety training. The 2026 baseline is to assume jailbreaks succeed and defend at the output and tool layers (Ch 23, §23.3).

**JSON schema** : A formal description of the expected JSON shape, used to drive constrained decoding. The contract between prompt and downstream code (Ch 7, §7.2).

**Judge model** : The LLM used to score outputs in LLM-as-judge eval. Should be different (and usually stronger) than the model being judged (Ch 5, §5.5).

**Judge rotation** : Periodically swapping the judge model to avoid correlated-family bias and detect drift in scoring (Ch 5, §5.6).


### K

**Kappa** : Cohen's kappa. Measures inter-rater agreement adjusted for chance. Used to validate that human raters (or LLM judges) agree on a rubric (Ch 4, §4.5).

**KG-RAG** : Knowledge-graph RAG. Retrieval augmented with traversals of a structured graph over entities and relations. Wins where queries require multi-hop reasoning (Ch 11, §11.3).

**Knowledge graph RAG** : See _KG-RAG_ (Ch 11, §11.3).

**Kong AI Gateway** : Enterprise API gateway with AI-specific features (model routing, prompt templates, semantic caching). Strong for organizations already on Kong (Ch 17, §17.3).

**Krippendorff's alpha** : Inter-rater agreement coefficient generalized across rater counts and scale types. Preferred over kappa when raters or items vary (Ch 4, §4.5).

**KV cache** : The stored key/value tensors from prior tokens in an attention computation. Re-used across decoding steps; what makes streaming cheap (Ch 2, §2.5).

**Key management** : Storing, rotating, and scoping provider API keys. The most common source of credential leaks in AI systems; centralize at the gateway (Ch 17, §17.6).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### L

**Langfuse** : Open-source LLM observability platform with strong tracing, eval integration, and prompt management. Common default for self-hosted observability (Ch 19, §19.3).

**LangGraph** : Graph-based agent orchestration framework from LangChain. State machines for agent workflows (Ch 15, §15.4).

**Late interaction** : Retrieval method (e.g., ColBERT, ColPali) that defers similarity computation to token-level pairs at query time. More accurate than bi-encoders, more expensive (Ch 12, §12.3).

**Latency budget** : The end-to-end time allowed for a user-facing response, decomposed by stage (network, retrieval, LLM, post-processing). Allocate explicitly (Ch 20, §20.2).

**Length bias** : LLM judges systematically prefer longer responses. Mitigated by length-controlled rubrics or pairwise prompts (Ch 5, §5.6).

**LiteLLM** : Open-source proxy that normalizes 100+ provider APIs behind an OpenAI-compatible interface. The build-it-yourself gateway baseline (Ch 17, §17.3).

**Llama** : Meta's open-weight model family, the de facto reference for open-source AI through 2026 (Ch 22, §22.1).

**llama.cpp** : C++ inference engine optimized for CPU and consumer GPUs. Powers most local AI tooling (Ch 22, §22.6).

**LLM-as-judge** : Using an LLM to score outputs against a rubric. Cheaper than human eval, but subject to position, length, and family bias (Ch 5, §5.5).

**Logit** : The pre-softmax score the model assigns to each possible next token. Direct logit access enables custom samplers and confidence proxies (Ch 2, §2.5).

**Long-term memory** : Agent memory that persists across sessions, typically stored externally (vector store, KG, SQL) and retrieved on demand (Ch 14, §14.5).

**LoRA** : Low-Rank Adaptation. Fine-tuning that learns small rank-decomposition matrices alongside frozen base weights. The dominant cost-efficient fine-tuning method (Ch 22, §22.3).

**Lost in the middle** : The empirical finding that LLMs attend less to content in the middle of long contexts. Argues for putting the most important material at the start or end (Ch 8, §8.5).

**Latent space** : The high-dimensional vector space where embeddings live. Operationally, "moving through latent space" means changing embeddings via query rewriting or fine-tuning (Ch 10, §10.1).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### M

**Matryoshka embedding** : Embeddings trained so any prefix is itself a useful (lower-dimensional) embedding. Lets you store full vectors but query at lower dim for speed (Ch 10, §10.3).

**max_tokens** : API parameter capping the length of the generated response. Set conservatively to bound cost and latency (Ch 3, §3.3).

**MCP** : Model Context Protocol. Open standard (Anthropic-introduced, now widely adopted) for connecting LLMs to tools and data sources through a common server interface (Ch 13).

**Memory architecture** : The design of an agent's scratchpad, episodic, and long-term memory subsystems and how they interact (Ch 14, §14.5).

**Message turn** : One exchange (user message + assistant response) within a multi-turn conversation. The unit of conversation API state (Ch 3, §3.1).

**MIPRO** : A DSPy optimizer that jointly tunes prompt instructions and few-shot examples. The serious-team alternative to hand-tuning (Ch 6, §6.3).

**Mistral** : French open-weight model family known for efficient mid-size models and the Mixtral MoE line (Ch 22, §22.1).

**MLX** : Apple's array framework optimized for Apple Silicon. The default inference stack on Mac and iPhone (Ch 22, §22.6).

**ML platform engineer** : Engineer who builds shared infrastructure for AI teams: training clusters, eval platforms, gateways, observability. Distinct from AI engineer (Ch 24, §24.1).

**Modal** : Serverless platform popular for batch inference, fine-tuning, and sandboxed code execution. Hybrid build/buy choice (Ch 22, §22.4).

**Model card** : Provider-published document describing a model's training, capabilities, limits, and safety properties. Required reading before adopting any new model (Ch 2, §2.9).

**Model Context Protocol** : See _MCP_ (Ch 13).

**Model upgrade workflow** : The repeatable process for evaluating, A/B testing, and rolling out a new model snapshot. Codified, not ad hoc (Ch 21, §21.6).

**MRR** : Mean Reciprocal Rank. Average of 1/rank-of-first-correct over a query set. Standard retrieval metric for "find the right thing" tasks (Ch 9, §9.5).

**Multi-agent** : A system composed of multiple LLM agents that interact via messages. Useful for well-decomposed problems; usually overkill (Ch 15).

**Multimodal RAG** : RAG over non-text modalities (images, PDFs as images, video, audio) using multimodal embeddings or page-level retrievers like ColPali (Ch 12, §12.6).

**Mixture of Experts** : Architecture where only a subset of model parameters activates per token, dramatically improving inference economics at fixed parameter count. Used by Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, and others (Ch 22, §22.2).

**MoE** : See _Mixture of Experts_ (Ch 22, §22.2).


### N

**Naive RAG** : The baseline pattern: embed query, retrieve top-k by vector similarity, stuff into prompt, generate. Insufficient for production but a useful starting point (Ch 9, §9.4).

**NDCG** : Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain. Retrieval metric that rewards highly relevant results at top ranks and discounts later positions (Ch 9, §9.5).

**NER** : Named Entity Recognition. Pre-LLM technique for tagging entities (people, places, dates); still useful for PII redaction and KG construction (Ch 19, §19.7).

**Nine-layer architecture** : See _9-layer architecture_ under "Z" / numeric section (Ch 16, §16.2).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### O

**Observability** : The collected practices (traces, logs, metrics, evals on production data) that let you understand what your AI system is doing in real time (Ch 19, §19.1).

**Observation validation** : Checking that tool outputs match expected schema and policy before feeding them back to the agent. The defense against tool-result-based injection (Ch 13, §13.5, Ch 23, §23.3).

**OCR** : Optical Character Recognition. Pre-step in many document RAG pipelines; in 2026 increasingly replaced by direct multimodal retrieval (ColPali) (Ch 12, §12.4).

**Ollama** : Local model runner with a simple CLI and library API. The default way to run open-weight models on a developer laptop (Ch 22, §22.6).

**On-device inference** : Running models on the user's device rather than a server. Trades model size for privacy, offline capability, and zero marginal cost (Ch 22, §22.6).

**OpenAI Realtime** : OpenAI's WebSocket-based real-time speech-to-speech API. Reference platform for low-latency voice agents (Ch 20, §20.5).

**Open-weight** : A model whose parameters are publicly downloadable, with or without a fully open license. The 2026 stack is built on a mix of closed-API and open-weight models (Ch 22, §22.1).

**Orchestrator-workers** : Multi-agent pattern where one agent dispatches subtasks to specialized workers and synthesizes results. The most reliable multi-agent topology (Ch 15, §15.2).

**OSWorld** : Benchmark for computer-use agents on real desktop tasks. Current scores show the gap between demo and production (Ch 15, §15.6).

**Output safety** : The class of safety checks applied to model output before it reaches users or tools: PII redaction, content filtering, refusal-classifier, schema validation (Ch 23, §23.2).

**Output validation** : Schema, policy, and semantic checks applied to outputs in code before downstream use. The last reliable line of defense (Ch 23, §23.3).

**Off-the-shelf model** : A model available through a hosted API requiring no training. The starting point for nearly every AI feature in 2026 (Ch 22, §22.1).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### P

**Paragraph hash** : A stable identifier for a chunk of source text used to attach and verify citations across re-indexings (Ch 11, §11.7).

**Per-tenant budget** : A cap on spend per customer enforced at the gateway. The cost discipline that prevents one tenant from draining your margins (Ch 17, §17.6).

**Percent agreement** : The fraction of items on which raters agree, ignoring chance. Simple but inflated; use kappa for serious analysis (Ch 4, §4.5).

**PEFT** : Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning. Family of methods (LoRA, QLoRA, prefix tuning, adapters) that update a small fraction of parameters (Ch 22, §22.3).

**pgvector** : PostgreSQL extension that adds vector types and indexes. The lowest-friction vector store for teams already on Postgres (Ch 10, §10.4).

**Phoenix** : Arize's open-source AI observability and eval tool. Strong on notebook-driven workflows (Ch 19, §19.3).

**PHI** : Protected Health Information. The HIPAA-defined category of identifiable health data; if you process it, you need BAAs and tight controls (Ch 19, §19.6).

**PII redaction** : Detecting and removing personally identifiable information from prompts, logs, or outputs. Combination of regex, NER, and LLM classification (Ch 19, §19.7).

**Pinecone** : Managed vector database with a strong production reputation. The "boring choice" for vector storage (Ch 10, §10.4).

**Plan-and-execute** : Agent pattern that first produces a complete plan, then executes steps with limited replanning. More predictable than ReAct, less adaptive (Ch 14, §14.2).

**Portkey** : Multi-provider AI gateway with focus on observability and prompt versioning. SaaS alternative to LiteLLM (Ch 17, §17.3).

**Position bias** : LLM judges prefer outputs in certain positions (often the first). Mitigated by randomizing presentation order (Ch 5, §5.6).

**Post-mortem culture** : Practice of blameless reviews of AI failures (bad answers, outages, cost spikes), with action items tracked to completion (Ch 23 §23.7; Ch 25 §25.2).

**Pretraining** : The initial training of a foundation model on a large unlabeled corpus. As an AI engineer, you almost never do this; you consume the outputs (Ch 2, §2.2).

**Private Cloud Compute** : Apple's privacy-preserving cloud architecture for AI workloads that exceed on-device capacity. Reference design for confidential AI infra (Ch 22, §22.6).

**Prompt caching** : Provider-side caching of the prefix of a request so subsequent calls with the same prefix skip recomputation. The biggest single cost lever in 2026 (Ch 18, §18.2).

**Prompt compression** : Reducing token count of a prompt while preserving meaning, via summarization, paraphrase, or learned compressors. Use after caching, not before (Ch 18, §18.7).

**Prompt engineering** : The craft of writing prompts that produce desired model behavior. Still relevant in 2026 but subsumed by _context engineering_ as the broader discipline (Ch 7, §7.1).

**Prompt injection** : Attack that manipulates the model via untrusted text in the prompt, causing it to ignore instructions or exfiltrate data. The defining LLM security threat (Ch 23, §23.3).

**Prompt registry** : Versioned store of prompts with metadata (author, eval results, deployment status). Source of truth, not strings in code (Ch 7, §7.4).

**Prompt version** : An immutable, addressable identifier for a specific prompt text. Required for reproducibility and rollback (Ch 7, §7.4).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
**Pydantic** : Python library for runtime validation of typed data. The standard way to define schemas and parse LLM JSON output in Python (Ch 7, §7.3).

**Pydantic AI** : Type-safe agent framework built on Pydantic. Light alternative to LangGraph/AutoGen for Python teams (Ch 15, §15.4).

**Provider** : A company offering hosted model inference (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, etc.). Treat provider choice as a routing parameter, not an architectural commitment (Ch 17, §17.2).

**Provider snapshot** : See _snapshot_ (Ch 3, §3.1).

**Production** : Any environment where real users depend on the system. In AI engineering, "production-ready" means evals pass, observability is on, costs are bounded, and there is a rollback plan (Ch 16).

**Prompt budget** : See _context budget_ (Ch 8, §8.2).


### Q

**Qdrant** : Open-source vector database written in Rust, popular for self-hosted production deployments (Ch 10, §10.4).

**QLoRA** : Quantized LoRA. Combines 4-bit base-model quantization with LoRA adapters, letting you fine-tune large models on a single GPU (Ch 22, §22.3).

**Query rewriting** : Reformulating the user's query before retrieval (decomposition, expansion, HyDE). The cheapest large retrieval gain (Ch 11, §11.2).

**Qwen** : Alibaba's open-weight model family. Strong on coding and Chinese tasks; competitive on English (Ch 22, §22.1).

**Quantization** : Reducing model weight precision (e.g., from FP16 to INT4) to shrink memory and speed inference, usually at small accuracy cost. Required for on-device and economical for large open models (Ch 22, §22.5).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### R

**RAG** : Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Pattern of fetching relevant content and including it in the prompt before generation. The dominant pattern for grounded answers (Ch 9).

**Rate limit** : Provider cap on request frequency. Enforced per minute (RPM) and per minute on tokens (TPM); plan capacity accordingly (Ch 3, §3.5).

**ReAct** : Reasoning-and-Acting loop: model thinks, picks a tool, observes the result, and repeats. The canonical agent pattern (Ch 13, §13.3).

**ReAct loop** : See _ReAct_ (Ch 13, §13.3).

**Recall@k** : Fraction of relevant items found in the top-k retrieved. The primary retrieval-stage quality metric (Ch 9, §9.5).

**Reciprocal Rank Fusion** : See _RRF_ (Ch 10, §10.5).

**Reference standard** : The "right answer" attached to each example in a golden set. Can be a specific string, a rubric, or a checker function (Ch 4, §4.3).

**Reflection** : Agent pattern where the model critiques its own output and decides whether to retry or revise. Useful for hard reasoning; doubles cost (Ch 14, §14.2).

**Refusal** : Model output declining to comply with a request, usually for safety, capability, or knowledge reasons. Behavior to be tuned, not eliminated (Ch 2, §2.3).

**Refusal pattern** : A reusable structure for how the system refuses or escalates: state the limit, suggest alternatives, escalate to human if available (Ch 23, §23.5).

**Regression detection** : Automatic alerting when an eval score drops below threshold for a new model, prompt, or pipeline change. The "did we just break something" signal (Ch 5, §5.7).

**Replicate** : Cloud platform for running open-weight and custom models behind an API. Lower friction than self-hosting; thinner control than Modal/Anyscale (Ch 22, §22.4).

**Reranker** : A cross-encoder or LLM that re-scores the top-N retrieved items for final ranking. The single biggest retrieval quality gain after hybrid search (Ch 11, §11.1).

**Request ID** : A unique identifier the provider returns for each call, used for support, deduplication, and tracing (Ch 3, §3.5).

**Response format** : API field declaring the expected output shape (text, JSON, structured). Often paired with a schema for constrained decoding (Ch 7, §7.2).

**Retry budget** : Maximum cumulative retries (count or time) for a single logical request. Prevents retry storms during provider outages (Ch 3, §3.5).

**RLHF** : Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. Aligns base models with human preferences via a learned reward model. Largely supplanted by DPO and variants in 2026 (Ch 2, §2.3).

**Role** : The speaker label on a message turn: `system`, `user`, `assistant`, or `tool`. Different providers enforce different role rules (Ch 3, §3.1).

**Routing tier** : A gateway component that picks the model/provider for a given request based on cost, latency, capability, or fallback rules (Ch 17, §17.4).

**RPM** : Requests Per Minute. A standard rate-limit unit (Ch 3, §3.5).

**RRF** : Reciprocal Rank Fusion. A simple, robust algorithm for combining ranked lists from multiple retrievers (e.g., BM25 + vector). The default fusion choice (Ch 10, §10.5).

**Rubric** : A structured scoring guide breaking quality into named criteria with anchors. The bridge from "I know it when I see it" to a usable eval (Ch 4, §4.4).

**Reasoning model** : An LLM with built-in extended-thinking mode (e.g., Claude with thinking, GPT o-series, DeepSeek R1). Higher cost and latency, better on hard analytic tasks (Ch 2, §2.3).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
**Retrieval pipeline** : The full chain from query to ranked context: parsing, rewriting, retrieving, reranking, and packing into the prompt (Ch 11).


### S

**Sampling** : Choosing the next token from the model's probability distribution rather than always picking the most likely. Controlled by temperature, top-p, top-k (Ch 2, §2.5).

**Sandbox** : An isolated execution environment for running untrusted code (LLM-generated or user-supplied). Required for any tool that runs code (Ch 13, §13.5).

**Scratchpad** : Short-term working memory an agent writes to during a task. Often the model's own visible reasoning or a dedicated scratch buffer (Ch 14, §14.5).

**Self-Refine** : Prompting pattern where the model produces an answer, critiques it, and revises. A specific instance of reflection (Ch 6, §6.2).

**Semantic caching** : Cache lookup that matches by embedding similarity rather than exact prefix. Higher hit rate, risk of returning wrong answers; deploy with care (Ch 18, §18.4).

**Semantic chunking** : Splitting documents by semantic boundaries (topic shifts) rather than by fixed token count. Improves retrieval coherence (Ch 9, §9.3).

**Silent reroute** : When a provider serves a different model than the requested alias without notification. The argument for dated versions (Ch 3, §3.11).

**Snapshot** : A specific dated build of a model that does not change. Pin to snapshots in production (Ch 3, §3.1).

**Span** : A timed segment inside a trace, representing one operation (model call, retrieval, tool execution). The unit of structured observability (Ch 19, §19.2).

**Stop sequence** : A string that, when produced, halts generation. Used to enforce output boundaries (Ch 3, §3.3).

**STT** : Speech-to-Text. The first stage of a classical voice pipeline. Latency here directly hits time-to-first-token (Ch 20, §20.3).

**Streaming** : Receiving tokens incrementally as they are generated. Required for UX latency; complicates retries and parsing (Ch 3, §3.2).

**Structured output** : Output that conforms to a declared schema (JSON, function call, etc.). The contract between LLM and downstream code (Ch 7, §7.1).

**System prompt** : The high-priority instruction message sent at the start of every conversation. Sets persona, rules, and tools. Cached aggressively (Ch 3, §3.1).

**Schema validation** : Verifying that an LLM-produced object conforms to a declared schema. Done in code, not in the prompt (Ch 7, §7.3).

**Spike** : See _feasibility spike_ (Ch 24, §24.6).

**Side effect** : An action a tool produces that changes external state (file write, payment, email). Side effects must be guarded by validation and often human-in-the-loop (Ch 13, §13.6).

**Sub-question** : A piece of a decomposed user query, retrieved or answered independently before synthesis. The mechanism behind multi-hop RAG (Ch 11, §11.5).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### T

**Telephony integration** : Connecting an AI voice agent to the phone network (SIP, Twilio, WebRTC bridges). Adds codec, network, and PSTN-specific concerns to the voice stack (Ch 20, §20.8).

**Temperature** : Sampling parameter that scales the logit distribution. 0 means greedy; higher values produce more diverse outputs (Ch 2, §2.5).

**TGI** : Text Generation Inference. Hugging Face's high-throughput serving engine for open-weight models. Common alternative to vLLM (Ch 22, §22.5).

**Time-to-first-token** : Latency from request send to first generated token. The user-perceived "thinking time" metric (Ch 20, §20.2).

**Together AI** : Cloud platform offering hosted open-weight models and fine-tuning. Common build-on-open-weights choice (Ch 22, §22.4).

**Token** : The unit of LLM input/output: a sub-word piece produced by the tokenizer. Pricing, context limits, and rate limits are all in tokens (Ch 2, §2.2).

**Token budget guardrail** : Pre-flight check that estimates request token count against caps and rejects or trims before sending (Ch 23, §23.1).

**Tokenizer** : The algorithm that maps text to tokens and back. Different models have different tokenizers; one Latin character ≠ one token (Ch 2, §2.2).

**Tool catalog** : The set of tools exposed to an agent for a given task. Smaller catalogs improve accuracy; larger ones improve capability (Ch 13, §13.4).

**Tool schema** : A formal description (usually JSON-Schema-style) of a tool's name, description, and parameters. The interface the agent sees (Ch 13, §13.2).

**Tool use** : The model's ability to call external functions during generation. The mechanism behind agents and most production LLM integrations (Ch 13, §13.1).

**top-k** : Sampling parameter restricting the next-token choice to the k most likely tokens (Ch 2, §2.5).

**top-p** : Nucleus sampling. Restricts the next-token choice to the smallest set whose cumulative probability exceeds p (Ch 2, §2.5).

**Toxic content** : Output containing harmful, harassing, or otherwise prohibited material. Detected by classifiers in the output-safety layer (Ch 23, §23.2).

**TPM** : Tokens Per Minute. A standard rate-limit unit, typically the binding constraint at scale (Ch 3, §3.5).

**Trace** : The full record of one logical request through the system, composed of nested spans. The unit of post-hoc debugging (Ch 19, §19.2).

**TTFT** : Time-to-First-Token. See _time-to-first-token_ (Ch 20, §20.2).

**TTS** : Text-to-Speech. The final stage of a classical voice pipeline. Choice of provider dominates perceived voice quality (Ch 20, §20.4).

**Transformer** : The neural architecture underlying virtually all modern LLMs, defined by self-attention over sequences. AI engineers rarely need to know the math; they do need to know its cost shape (Ch 2, §2.1).

**Tail latency** : The 95th-, 99th-, or 99.9th-percentile response time. The metric users actually feel; mean latency hides it (Ch 17, §17.5).


### U

**Untrusted-content tagging** : Marking retrieved or tool-fetched text as untrusted in the prompt (e.g., wrapping in `<untrusted>` blocks) so the model treats it as data, not instructions. Partial defense against indirect injection (Ch 23, §23.3).

**User message** : A message turn produced by the end user. The primary "untrusted input" surface in an LLM system (Ch 3, §3.1).

blocks.en_title: Appendix C — Glossary
blocks.src:
### V

**Vector database** : A store optimized for nearest-neighbor search over high-dimensional vectors. Backbone of most RAG systems (Ch 10, §10.4).

**Vision token** : A patch of a tokenized image that occupies "token slots" in a multimodal model's context. Pricing and context limits apply (Ch 12, §12.4).

**vLLM** : High-throughput open-source inference engine with PagedAttention and continuous batching. The reference choice for self-hosting open-weight models (Ch 22, §22.5).
