**Vendor lock-in** : The cost of switching providers, in code changes, eval revalidation, and feature parity. Gateways and abstraction layers minimize but do not eliminate it (Ch 17, §17.2).

**Voice agent** : An LLM system that interacts via spoken language, typically composed of STT + LLM + TTS or an end-to-end voice model (Ch 20).


### W

**Weaviate** : Open-source vector database with strong hybrid search and modules system. Common self-hosted choice (Ch 10, §10.4).

**Weighted kappa** : Kappa variant that penalizes large disagreements more than small ones, appropriate for ordinal rubrics (e.g., 1-5 scales) (Ch 4, §4.5).

**Workflow** : A scripted multi-step LLM pipeline with deterministic control flow. Distinct from an agent, which decides its own control flow (Ch 13, §13.1).


### X

**X-request-id** : Common header name for the per-request identifier returned by providers. See _request ID_ (Ch 3, §3.5).

**XML tags** : A common convention for delimiting prompt sections (`<context>`, `<instructions>`, `<untrusted>`). Tends to outperform Markdown delimiters for instruction adherence on Claude and several other models (Ch 8, §8.2).


### Y

**YAML** : A common config format used for prompts, eval definitions, and pipeline configs in AI tooling. Choose YAML for human-edited configs, JSON for machine-produced ones (Ch 7, §7.4).


### Z

**Zero-shot** : Asking the model to perform a task without examples, relying on instruction alone. The starting point for most prompts; reach for few-shot or fine-tuning only when zero-shot scores fall short (Ch 6, §6.2).

* * *


### Numeric

**9-layer architecture** : The reference decomposition of a production LLM system into nine layers (intake, gateway, prompt, retrieval, model, tool, memory, safety, observability). Map your stack to it (Ch 16, §16.2).

---

blocks.en_title: Appendix D — Anti-Patterns Cheat Sheet
blocks.src:
A printable summary of the seven anti-patterns from Chapter 25, designed to be referenced quickly during architecture reviews, design docs, and feature scoping. Pin this to the wall by your desk. When a teammate proposes an AI feature, walk down the table and ask which row they're closest to falling into. If the answer is "none," ask again; the honest answer is usually "two of them."

The cheat sheet is intentionally denser than the chapter. The chapter argues the case; this page is the operational summary.


### Quick reference

| # | Anti-pattern | The kill criterion | Anchor failure | Chapter(s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Shipping without evals | If you can't articulate measurable success, the feature shouldn't ship. | Air Canada (Thread B Failure 1) | Ch 4 |
| 2 | Over-engineering with frameworks | If the framework abstracts something you need direct control over, don't use the framework for that layer. | (no canonical — death by a thousand cuts) | Ch 15, Ch 16 |
| 3 | Treating LLM outputs as deterministic | If your code can't handle an unexpected response, it isn't production-ready. | Google AI Overviews (Failure 2) | Ch 2, Ch 7 |
| 4 | Ignoring the cost dimension | If you can't say what a feature costs per active user per day, you don't have cost discipline. | Fine-tune deprecation cascade (Failure 4, anchored Ch 22) | Ch 17, Ch 18 (discipline); Ch 22 (anchor) |
| 5 | Trusting LLM-as-judge without validation | If your judge hasn't been calibrated against humans at κ ≥ 0.6 on ≥ 50 cases, the eval isn't production-grade. | (no canonical — correlated-family bias) | Ch 4, Ch 11 |
| 6 | Building agents when workflows suffice | If you can specify the task as deterministic steps with at most one LLM call per step, don't agent-ify it. | 52K USD overnight agent (Failure 5); 2026 agentic recursion (Failure 6) | Ch 14, Ch 15 |
| 7 | Shipping without safety architecture | If you have a multi-tenant or RAG system without the four-layer defense (§23.3), you have a known unaddressed threat. | 2025 prompt-injection-in-production incident (Failure 3) | Ch 23 |
  

### The seven anti-patterns in detail

blocks.en_title: Appendix D — Anti-Patterns Cheat Sheet
blocks.src:
#### Anti-pattern 1: Shipping without evals

**The pattern.** AI features ship on team intuition. The eval is _we tried a few prompts and it seemed to work._ There is no graded set, no regression gate, no signal when a model upgrade silently changes behavior.

**How teams fall into it.** The team is small, the deadline is tight, the demo went well. Evals feel like the kind of overhead a more mature team would add later. They also feel hard to write: the team isn't sure what "good" looks like in measurable terms, so writing the eval feels like solving the product problem twice. So they ship, planning to add evals once the feature stabilizes. The feature never stabilizes.

**Symptoms.** Bug reports describe quality regressions the team can't reproduce. Prompts get tweaked based on the most recent complaint. Model upgrades are scary because no one knows what they'll change. The phrase _it used to work better_ appears in standups.

**The discipline.** Eval-driven development (Chapter 4). Treat the eval as the executable specification of the feature — written before or alongside the implementation, run on every change, blocking on regression. Start with 20 to 50 hand-graded cases; grow the set as failures appear in production.

**Anchor.** Air Canada (Thread B Failure 1). The airline's chatbot promised a refund policy that didn't exist; the tribunal ruled the chatbot's outputs were company statements. The company had no systematic way to know what statements it was making. That is the cost of no evals at scale.

**Kill criterion.** If you can't articulate what success looks like in measurable terms — not "users will love it" but "≥ 85% on the graded set, no regression on the failure set" — the feature shouldn't ship until you can. Articulating the criterion is half the work of writing the eval.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D — Anti-Patterns Cheat Sheet
blocks.src:
#### Anti-pattern 2: Over-engineering with frameworks

**The pattern.** The team reaches for LangChain (or LlamaIndex, or whatever the current heavy framework is) reflexively. The framework's abstractions become the engineering surface. Every customization is a fight: monkey-patching, subclassing, reading source to figure out which callback fires when. The team is no longer building product; it's building around the framework.

**How teams fall into it.** The framework looks like leverage. Its README shows a three-line RAG pipeline. The team doesn't realize that the three-line version is the only version that's three lines; everything past the README is bespoke. By the time they discover this, they've built a system that's 70% framework integration code and 30% domain logic. The migration cost feels too high to walk back.

**Symptoms.** Onboarding new engineers takes weeks because they have to learn the framework before they can learn the product. PRs are reviewed for framework-correctness more than product-correctness. Upgrading the framework version is a quarterly event with its own project plan. Debugging a single LLM call requires tracing through six layers of abstraction.

**The discipline.** Start with primitives (Chapter 15, Chapter 16). The provider SDK, a prompt template, a Pydantic schema, an HTTP client. Add abstraction only when the same pattern appears in three places. Prefer Pydantic AI or a hand-rolled orchestrator over heavy frameworks for small teams. Layered architecture beats framework-driven architecture for most products.

**Anchor.** No single canonical failure — this anti-pattern kills by a thousand cuts. The shape is framework debt that accumulates until the team is spending more time on the framework than the product, and the cost is measured in months of velocity loss rather than a single bad headline.

**Kill criterion.** If the framework abstracts something you need direct control over — the prompt, the retry policy, the streaming protocol, the tool-call format — don't use the framework for that layer. Drop to primitives for that layer specifically, even if you keep the framework elsewhere.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D — Anti-Patterns Cheat Sheet
blocks.src:
#### Anti-pattern 3: Treating LLM outputs as deterministic

**The pattern.** Code reads LLM responses and dispatches on them as if they were stable function returns. No schema validation. No error variants. No confidence calibration. The 99% case works; the 1% case crashes the application or, worse, silently produces a bad result.

**How teams fall into it.** The first prompt the engineer writes happens to produce consistent JSON. They build on that. They don't add validation because it always works in dev. The first time production traffic hits the 1% case — an unusual user input, a model update, a refusal — the code blows up in a way that's hard to attribute.

**Symptoms.** Try/except blocks around `json.loads(llm_response)`. Comments saying _the model usually returns the right format_. Production logs full of `KeyError` and `ValidationError`. Customer reports of features that "just didn't do anything" — the LLM emitted a refusal, the code didn't handle it, the feature silently no-op'd.

**The discipline.** Engineer against a stochastic component (Chapter 2). Structured output with discriminated unions: success, error, refusal as distinct variants the type system forces you to handle (Chapter 7). Schema validation at the boundary. Confidence calibration where decisions branch on the LLM's certainty.

**Anchor.** Google AI Overviews (Thread B Failure 2). The "glue on pizza" answer was the retrieval layer feeding Reddit content to the model and the model treating it as authoritative — no validation, no source-quality gating, no absurdity detector. Same root failure: the system assumed its inputs and outputs were better-behaved than they were.

**Kill criterion.** If your code can't handle the LLM emitting an unexpected response — wrong schema, refusal, empty answer, hallucinated field — the code isn't production-ready. Production-readiness is defined by behavior on the 1% case, not the 99% case.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D — Anti-Patterns Cheat Sheet
blocks.src:
#### Anti-pattern 4: Ignoring the cost dimension

**The pattern.** AI features ship without per-feature cost tracking. The bill arrives at end-of-month and surprises someone. The team has no levers — no routing, no caching, no batching, no per-tenant attribution — and so no way to optimize when the cost spikes.

**How teams fall into it.** Inference costs are small at launch. A thousand users at five calls each on a cheap model is rounding-error on the cloud bill. The team is solving correctness, not cost. Then usage grows ten-fold, the team switches to a stronger model for quality, a new feature uses long context, and the bill becomes a finance conversation. By then the system has no cost levers because none were designed in.

**Symptoms.** No per-tenant cost dashboard. No routing layer between the application and the model. Every call goes to the same (usually most expensive) model. The team can't answer _what does this feature cost per active user per day?_ without a spreadsheet and an afternoon. Cost-reduction proposals are met with _we don't know what we'd save._

**The discipline.** Routing as the biggest cost lever (Chapter 17): cheap model first, escalate on uncertainty. Per-feature, per-tenant, per-call cost tracking (Chapter 18). Caching for repeated prompts. Batching where latency permits. Model-upgrade discipline that anticipates the cost shape of new releases.

**Anchor.** Fine-tune deprecation cascade (Thread B Failure 4). A team's GPT-4 fine-tunes became worse than GPT-5 base on the day GPT-5 shipped. Six to eight engineer-weeks of emergency migration followed. Systematic model-upgrade tracking would have anticipated the deprecation date and budgeted the migration; the team had neither.

**Kill criterion.** If you can't say what a feature costs per active user per day — and per active tenant per month — you don't have cost discipline. Building that visibility is a precondition to optimization, not a follow-up to it.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D — Anti-Patterns Cheat Sheet
blocks.src:
#### Anti-pattern 5: Trusting LLM-as-judge without validation

**The pattern.** The team uses an LLM to score outputs in their eval (Chapter 4 §4.5). The judge has never been calibrated against human labels. The eval scores look good. The team believes the system is working. Production behavior says otherwise; the eval was scoring what the LLM thinks "good" looks like, not what users do.

**How teams fall into it.** LLM-as-judge is too convenient to resist. Hand-grading is slow; an LLM judge scales to thousands of cases for dollars. The first batch of scores looks reasonable on inspection, so the team adopts the judge as the eval gate. They never circle back to validate against humans.

**Symptoms.** Eval scores trend up while user satisfaction is flat or down. The judge agrees with itself across model upgrades — because the judge and the system under test share the same family of biases. New eval cases are written by the same engineer who tunes the judge prompt, creating a feedback loop that gradually drifts away from human judgment.

**The discipline.** Eval discipline (Chapter 4) treats the judge as a hypothesis: it must be validated against humans on a meaningful set before it's allowed to gate anything. Multi-axis RAG eval (Chapter 11) decomposes "good answer" into faithfulness, relevance, completeness, and grounding so the judge has explicit criteria rather than a vibe.

**Anchor.** No single canonical failure — this one shows up as correlated-family bias, the recurring shape where the judge and the system under test share training data, training objectives, or family-level stylistic preferences, and the eval is therefore measuring agreement rather than quality. The failure is quiet by design: the team is reassured by the wrong signal.

**Kill criterion.** If your LLM judge hasn't been validated against humans on at least 50 cases with κ ≥ 0.6 agreement (and ideally against humans of different stripes — engineer, domain expert, user), the eval is not production-grade. Treat the judge the way you'd treat any other model: held-out test set, periodic recalibration, drift detection.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D — Anti-Patterns Cheat Sheet
blocks.src:
#### Anti-pattern 6: Building agents when workflows suffice

**The pattern.** The team reaches for a multi-agent or agentic architecture for a problem a simple deterministic workflow would handle. They treat _agentic_ as inherently more sophisticated than _workflow_ , which is exactly backwards: a workflow is the production-hardened version of an agent for tasks that decompose into known steps.

**How teams fall into it.** Agents are exciting. The team has just read a paper. The product manager wants to ship something that sounds modern. The architectural decision is driven by aesthetics rather than by the task's structure. Once committed, the team accumulates orchestration, retry, bound, and observability complexity that the workflow would have made implicit.

**Symptoms.** Unbounded loops. Tool calls that fire when they shouldn't. Cost spikes that no one can predict. Debugging sessions that involve replaying trajectories rather than reading logs. The phrase _the agent decided to_ in incident post-mortems — the agent is being treated as a quasi-employee whose decisions are described rather than diagnosed.

**The discipline.** First ask whether the task is an agent at all (Chapter 14). Most production tasks aren't: they're sequences of deterministic steps with at most one LLM call per step, which is the definition of a workflow. If you do need an agent, bound it: iteration cap, cost circuit breaker, per-tool circuit breaker, tool-call deduplication, observation validation — all in place before any production traffic (Chapter 14). For multi-agent specifically, orchestrator-and-workers beats peer-to-peer for almost every production case (Chapter 15).

**Anchor.** Two anchors at different scales of the same failure class. The 52K USD overnight agent (Thread B Failure 5, Chapter 14) is the single-agent case: no iteration cap, no cost circuit breaker, no tool-call dedup; the agent ran for fourteen hours emitting the same expensive calls before anyone noticed. The 2026 agentic recursion incident (Thread B Failure 6, Chapter 15) is the multi-agent case: an orchestrator-and-workers system converged on a wrong intermediate answer and doubled its token consumption per retry loop. Both failures are the same shape — an agentic system without the bounds a deterministic workflow would have made implicit — surfacing at different scales of architecture.

**Kill criterion.** If you can specify your task as a sequence of deterministic steps with at most one LLM call per step, you have a workflow; don't agent-ify it. If you do have a real agent, every one of {iteration cap, cost circuit breaker, per-tool circuit breaker, tool-call deduplication, observation validation} must be in place before the agent ever sees production traffic. Missing one is not "we'll add it next sprint" — it is a gate on shipping.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D — Anti-Patterns Cheat Sheet
blocks.src:
#### Anti-pattern 7: Shipping without safety architecture

**The pattern.** A multi-tenant or RAG-backed AI system goes to production with one layer of defense — usually the model's own training-time refusals. The system works on benign traffic. The first sophisticated adversarial input — typically arriving as untrusted content inside a retrieved document, a tool output, or a user upload — gets through and exfiltrates data, takes unauthorized actions, or reveals the system prompt.

**How teams fall into it.** Prompt injection feels like a threat that the model vendor handles. The team's threat model is built around direct user input ("ignore previous instructions"), which the model refuses. They don't realize that indirect prompt injection — instructions hidden in a PDF the user uploads, in a tool's JSON output, in a web page the agent browses — is the dominant 2025–2026 threat shape and that the model's refusals are one layer of defense, not a complete one.

**Symptoms.** Threat-model docs that mention "prompt injection" once and then move on. No untrusted-content tagging in the prompt. No output validation that catches data exfiltration patterns. RAG systems with no provenance metadata propagated alongside retrieved chunks. Agents with tool access that aren't sandboxed at the execution layer.

**The discipline.** The four-layer prompt-injection defense (Chapter 23 §23.3): in-context defense (untrusted content explicitly marked, instructions in the system prompt only), output validation (catch exfiltration shapes, PII patterns, unexpected tool calls), untrusted-content tagging (every retrieved or tool-sourced token tagged with provenance, never treated as instruction), and indirect-injection mitigations (sandboxed tool execution, policy gates, cross-tenant isolation). Tool execution sandboxed at the layer below the model (Chapter 13). Observability that surfaces unusual cross-tenant patterns (Chapter 19).

**Anchor.** The 2025 prompt-injection-in-production incident (Thread B Failure 3, Chapter 23). A malicious customer uploaded a document with hidden instructions; the document was retrieved into an enterprise customer-service agent's context; the agent followed the instructions and emitted another customer's data. The company's BAAs, the model's own refusals, and the eval suite all failed to catch it — each was a single layer, and the attack threaded between them. The four-layer pattern emerged from the industry's response to this class of incident.

**Kill criterion.** If you have a multi-tenant system, a RAG system, or any agent that processes untrusted content, and you don't have all four layers of §23.3 in place, you have a known unaddressed threat class. Ship with the layers in place or don't ship. There is no "we'll add safety in v2" version of this anti-pattern that ends well.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D — Anti-Patterns Cheat Sheet
blocks.src:
### The team-level checklist

A tech lead can ask their team to self-assess against these. If the team answers _no_ to any of them, the team is in one of the anti-patterns; the cell in the table above points to which one.

* For every production AI feature, we have an eval that runs on every change and blocks merges on regression.
* We can state, today, what each production feature costs per active user per day and per active tenant per month.
* Every LLM call returns a structured response with discriminated success / error / refusal variants the type system forces us to handle.
* Every LLM call is traced; trajectory-level observability exists for our agents.
* Every agent in production has all of {iteration cap, cost circuit breaker, per-tool circuit breaker, tool-call deduplication, observation validation}.
* Our prompts live in a versioned registry, not as inline strings scattered across the codebase.
* Our LLM-as-judge has been calibrated against humans on ≥ 50 cases with κ ≥ 0.6, and we recalibrate at every model upgrade.
* We have a multi-provider routing layer; we are not single-provider locked-in.
* We have all four layers of the prompt-injection defense (§23.3) in every place we process untrusted content.
* We have a _can we eval this?_ gate at feature scoping, and we have killed features at that gate.
* We have executed a real model-upgrade workflow at least once and would not be surprised by the next deprecation.
* We have an incident post-mortem culture; every Sev-2-or-worse incident produces at least one new eval case.

Twelve _yes_ answers is the 2026 production-AI engineering competency level. Most teams answer _yes_ to six or seven and have a clear list of what to fix. The point of the checklist isn't to grade the team; it's to make the gaps specific enough to be staffed.


### A note on inverse anti-patterns

Not every team is at risk of all seven. The team at risk of anti-pattern 2 (over-engineering with frameworks) is often the same team _not_ at risk of anti-pattern 1 (shipping without evals): they over-build everywhere, including the eval layer, and their problem is velocity, not quality. The team at risk of anti-pattern 1 is often _not_ at risk of anti-pattern 2: they ship lean and fast and don't reach for frameworks; their problem is the missing measurement layer that would tell them when _fast_ became _broken_.

The same inversion shows up between anti-pattern 6 (building agents when workflows suffice) and the unstated inverse — the team that under-builds, leaves capability on the table by sticking with rigid workflows where a bounded agent would serve users better. Most failure modes have a mirror failure mode, and the engineering judgment is recognizing which side of the mirror your team is on.

The cheat sheet is a screening tool, not a checklist to satisfy. Pick the two or three anti-patterns your team is genuinely at risk of — usually they cluster by team culture: the cautious team risks 2 and 6 in their over-engineered forms; the move-fast team risks 1, 3, and 7 in their under-engineered forms; almost every team risks 4 and 5 because cost and eval calibration are quiet failures that don't announce themselves — and engineer against those specifically. Trying to defend against all seven equally is itself a form of anti-pattern 2.
